items.title: Inkling 2 Mini 的 GPU 实测出炉：llama.cpp 解码只有 Gemma 三成速度，开发者自研引擎把单张 RTX 3090 推到 129.5 tok/s
items.location: 中有 45～46 个位置的首选 token 一致
items.summary: Inkling 2 Mini 的 GPU 实测出炉：llama.cpp 解码只有 Gemma 三成速度，开发者自研引擎把单张 RTX 3090 推到 129.5 tok/s 资讯 AREX 2026-11-22 04:40 分享 以下文章来源于arex-research.com Inkling 2 Mini 开放权重释出次日，两份针对 NVIDIA 显卡的独立实测在 11 月 21 日先后贴出：一份针对现成 llama.cpp 测得慢速并定位原因，另一份给出自研引擎的加速结果。日本开发者 orenoa（@orenoa7）在 RTX 5090 实测帖 中写道，这个模型并没有出现「因为是 MoE 所以爆速」的情况：256K 输入下，解码只有 43～57 tok/s，约为同尺寸 Gemma 4 26B-A4B 的 32%，与稠密的 Qwen3.8 27B 相当。约 5 个小时后，开发者 Alexey Fateev（@superalesha）在 另一条帖子 里发布了自建 CUDA 引擎 maya-ik2 的成绩：单张 RTX 3090 上解码 129.5 tok/s，较 llama.cpp 快 2.3 倍，GSM8K 质量对照为 74/96 对 73/96，代码已在 GitHub 公开 。两份数据均为作者自报，尚无第三方复核。 Inkling 2 Mini 是 Thinking Machines Lab 于 11 月 20 日发布的开放权重 MoE（Mixture-of-Experts，混合专家）模型：总参数 26.4B、每 token 激活 3.4B，采用循环变压器（looped transformer）架构，中间层每个 token 循环执行三次，多数权重以 NVFP4 原生训练与部署，官方称总内存占用约 20 GB、可在消费级笔记本上离线运行（ 发布博客 ）。博客里用于对比的解码速度是按 614 GB/s 理论带宽推算的上限（BF16 权重、batch size 1、计入循环重复读取），并非实测。11 月 21 日，Rapid-MLX 也给出了 Mac 侧实测：M5 Max 36GB、4-bit 量化下单流 43 tok/s、峰值内存 23 GB（ 推文 ）。 RTX 5090 实测：现成 llama.cpp 只跑出 Gemma 的三成解码速度 orenoa7 的测试条

11 月 21 日先后贴出：一份针对现成 llama.cpp 测得慢速并定位原因，另一份给出自研引擎的加速结果。日本开发者 orenoa（@orenoa7）在 RTX 5090 实测帖 中写道，这个模型并没有出现「因为是 MoE 所以爆速」的情况：256K 输入下，解码只有 43～57 tok/s，约为同尺寸 Gemma 4 26B-A4B 的 32%，与稠密的 Qwen3.8 27B 相当。约 5 个小时后，开发者 Alexey Fateev（@superalesha）在 另一条帖子 里发布了自建 CUDA 引擎 maya-ik2 的成绩：单张 RTX 3090 上解码 129.5 tok/s，较 llama.cpp 快 2.3 倍，GSM8K 质量对照为 74/96 对 73/96，代码已在 GitHub 公开 。两份数据均为作者自报，尚无第三方复核。 Inkling 2 Mini 是 Thinking Machines Lab 于 11 月 20 日发布的开放权重 MoE（Mixture-of-Experts，混合专家）模型：总参数 26.4B、每 token 激活 3.4B，采用循环变压器（looped transformer）架构，中间层每个 token 循环执行三次，多数权重以 NVFP4 原生训练与部署，官方称总内存占用约 20 GB、可在消费级笔记本上离线运行（ 发布博客 ）。博客里用于对比的解码速度是按 614 GB/s 理论带宽推算的上限（BF16 权重、batch size 1、计入循环重复读取），并非实测。11 月 21 日，Rapid-MLX 也给出了 Mac 侧实测：M5 Max 36GB、4-bit 量化下单流 43 tok/s、峰值内存 23 GB（ 推文 ）。 RTX 5090 实测：现成 llama.cpp 只跑出 Gemma 的三成解码速度 orenoa7 的测试条件列得完整：RTX 5090 32GB（400W），Inkling 2 Mini、Gemma 4 26B-A4B、Qwen3.8 27B 三款模型都用 Unsloth 的 GGUF 量化（Inkling 为 UD-Q4_K_XL，17.6 GB），推理引擎是自行编译、加入 Inkling 支持的 llama.cpp（unsloth 版 b12588），上下文设 262,144，输出 1,024 token，greedy（贪心）解码、关闭思考模式，草稿模型（draft）全开：Inkling 用官方 dspark，Gemma 与 Qwen 用 MTP（多 token 预测），每个测试点取 5 次运行的中位数。 在约 25 万 token 输入下，Inkling 2 Mini 的 prefill（对输入的预填充处理）为 1,630 tok/s，prose（普通文本）解码 43 tok/s、code（代码）解码 57 tok/s。同样条件下，Gemma 4 26B-A4B 为 prefill 3,348、prose 137、code 176，Inkling 2 Mini 分别只有它的 49%、32%、32%；稠密的 Qwen3.8 27B 为 prefill 1,353、prose 52、code 69，Inkling 2 Mini 为其 120%、82%、82%。他同时提醒，这次是让模型在 llama.cpp 里原样运行，「优化之后应该还有改进余地」，RTX 3060 12GB 与 DGX Spark 上的实测仍在进行。 nsys 剖出的瓶颈：每 token 约 7,370 次内核调用，attention 之外占去 prefill 八成 orenoa7 用 NVIDIA 的 nsys 性能分析器追问慢的原因。Inkling 2 Mini 共 24 层，中央 12 层（第 6～17 层）每个 token 各循环 3 次，全模型每 token 计 48 次层访问；名义激活 3.4B，计入循环后每 token 权重激活 5.4B，与官方博客的口径一致。解码阶段的直接代价是内核调用次数：Inkling 每 token 约 7,370 次，约为 Gemma（约 1,260 次）的 6 倍。 Prefill 侧的原因不同：Inkling 存在 Gemma 没有的非量化矩阵运算，他还推测有 attention 参照表从 CPU 向 GPU 传输。对 256K prefill 的耗时拆解显示，Gemma 的处理时间里 attention 约占八成，Inkling 的 attention 只占约两成，其余全是 attention 之外的开销。这也解释了两组曲线的不同形状：输入从 8K 加到 256K，Gemma 的 prefill 从约 10,900 掉到 3,348 tok/s（降 69%），Inkling 只从约 2,080 缓降到 1,630（降 22%），衰减更平缓，但起点就低。 maya-ik2：把 7,350 次内核启动压进单个 CUDA 图 superalesha 对慢因的诊断与 orenoa7 的测量对得上：llama.cpp 在他的 RTX 3090 上每 token 发起约 7,350 次内核启动，一半以上的解码时间耗在 1～2 微秒的胶水算子上，模型只以 57 tok/s「爬行」。这个数字与 orenoa7 在 RTX 5090 上测得的约 7,370 次几乎一致，两份独立测量从两个方向指向同一瓶颈。 maya-ik2（基于 @PeasantSmith 的 Project Maya 构建）的主要改动有三项：3,072 个专家全部常驻显存（共 14.7 GiB），回答期间不再从内存或磁盘读取；整段计算重放进单个 CUDA 图（CUDA Graph），把每 token 约 7,350 次启动压到 781 次（README 当前写作 757 次）；自写 Tensor Core 内核，FP8 KV（键值缓存）attention 达 776 GB/s，NVFP4 专家内核在寄存器里把 4-bit 权重即时解包成 FP16、喂给 FP16 Tensor Core（745 GB/s），因为 RTX 3090 没有 FP4 硬件。BF16 视觉编码器挪到 CPU（处理新图像 4.5 秒、缓存命中 0.5 秒），腾出的 1.3 GB 显存换来 344K 上下文容量。 他的成绩单：短上下文解码 128.7 tok/s（HTTP 服务口径 129.5）对 llama.cpp 的 57.0；4K 输入解码 124.2、prefill 2,742 对 1,052；64K 时 105.6、prefill 2,361，llama.cpp 为 42.7 与 630，prefill 差距在此拉到 3.7 倍；128K 时 90.6、2,079；上下文加到 340K 仍有 62.3 tok/s，峰值显存 23.57 GiB。仓库 README 另给出官方 3 层 DSpark 草稿模型的投机解码成绩：文档编辑场景最高 212 tok/s。限制也写在明处：一次只服务一个请求；引擎只读 UD-Q4_K_XL 量化；48 次层访问中有 8 次要对全前缀做 attention，解码速度随上下文加深而下降。 质量对照已给出，第三方复核还没有 「零质量损失」是 superalesha 的口径，依据是他贴出的对照：96 道 GSM8K 题 greedy 解码，maya-ik2 得 74/96，标量路径 73/96，KL 散度 items.raw_text: Inkling 2 Mini 的 GPU 实测出炉：llama.cpp 解码只有 Gemma 三成速度，开发者自研引擎把单张 RTX 3090 推到 129.5 tok/s 资讯 AREX 2026-11-22 04:40 分享 以下文章来源于arex-research.com Inkling 2 Mini 开放权重释出次日，两份针对 NVIDIA 显卡的独立实测在 11 月 21 日先后贴出：一份针对现成 llama.cpp 测得慢速并定位原因，另一份给出自研引擎的加速结果。日本开发者 orenoa（@orenoa7）在 RTX 5090 实测帖 中写道，这个模型并没有出现「因为是 MoE 所以爆速」的情况：256K 输入下，解码只有 43～57 tok/s，约为同尺寸 Gemma 4 26B-A4B 的 32%，与稠密的 Qwen3.8 27B 相当。约 5 个小时后，开发者 Alexey Fateev（@superalesha）在 另一条帖子 里发布了自建 CUDA 引擎 maya-ik2 的成绩：单张 RTX 3090 上解码 129.5 tok/s，较 llama.cpp 快 2.3 倍，GSM8K 质量对照为 74/96 对 73/96，代码已在 GitHub 公开 。两份数据均为作者自报，尚无第三方复核。 Inkling 2 Mini 是 Thinking Machines Lab 于 11 月 20 日发布的开放权重 MoE（Mixture-of-Experts，混合专家）模型：总参数 26.4B、每 token 激活 3.4B，采用循环变压器（looped transformer）架构，中间层每个 token 循环执行三次，多数权重以 NVFP4 原生训练与部署，官方称总内存占用约 20 GB、可在消费级笔记本上离线运行（ 发布博客 ）。博客里用于对比的解码速度是按 614 GB/s 理论带宽推算的上限（BF16 权重、batch size 1、计入循环重复读取），并非实测。11 月 21 日，Rapid-MLX 也给出了 Mac 侧实测：M5 Max 36GB、4-bit 量化下单流 43 tok/s、峰值内存 23 GB（ 推文 ）。 RTX 5090 实测：现成 llama.cpp 只跑出 Gemma 的三成解码速度 orenoa7 的测试条件列得完整：RTX 5090 32GB（400W），Inkling 2 Mini、Gemma 4 26B-A4B、Qwen3.8 27B 三款模型都用 Unsloth 的 GGUF 量化（Inkling 为 UD-Q4_K_XL，17.6 GB），推理引擎是自行编译、加入 Inkling 支持的 llama.cpp（unsloth 版 b12588），上下文设 262,144，输出 1,024 token，greedy（贪心）解码、关闭思考模式，草稿模型（draft）全开：Inkling 用官方 dspark，Gemma 与 Qwen 用 MTP（多 token 预测），每个测试点取 5 次运行的中位数。 在约 25 万 token 输入下，Inkling 2 Mini 的 prefill（对输入的预填充处理）为 1,630 tok/s，prose（普通文本）解码 43 tok/s、code（代码）解码 57 tok/s。同样条件下，Gemma 4 26B-A4B 为 prefill 3,348、prose 137、code 176，Inkling 2 Mini 分别只有它的 49%、32%、32%；稠密的 Qwen3.8 27B 为 prefill 1,353、prose 52、code 69，Inkling 2 Mini 为其 120%、82%、82%。他同时提醒，这次是让模型在 llama.cpp 里原样运行，「优化之后应该还有改进余地」，RTX 3060 12GB 与 DGX Spark 上的实测仍在进行。 nsys 剖出的瓶颈：每 token 约 7,370 次内核调用，attention 之外占去 prefill 八成 orenoa7 用 NVIDIA 的 nsys 性能分析器追问慢的原因。Inkling 2 Mini 共 24 层，中央 12 层（第 6～17 层）每个 token 各循环 3 次，全模型每 token 计 48 次层访问；名义激活 3.4B，计入循环后每 token 权重激活 5.4B，与官方博客的口径一致。解码阶段的直接代价是内核调用次数：Inkling 每 token 约 7,370 次，约为 Gemma（约 1,260 次）的 6 倍。 Prefill 侧的原因不同：Inkling 存在 Gemma 没有的非量化矩阵运算，他还推测有 attention 参照表从 CPU 向 GPU 传输。对 256K prefill 的耗时拆解显示，Gemma 的处理时间里 attention 约占八成，Inkling 的 attention 只占约两成，其余全是 attention 之外的开销。这也解释了两组曲线的不同形状：输入从 8K 加到 256K，Gemma 的 prefill 从约 10,900 掉到 3,348 tok/s（降 69%），Inkling 只从约 2,080 缓降到 1,630（降 22%），衰减更平缓，但起点就低。 maya-ik2：把 7,350 次内核启动压进单个 CUDA 图 superalesha 对慢因的诊断与 orenoa7 的测量对得上：llama.cpp 在他的 RTX 3090 上每 token 发起约 7,350 次内核启动，一半以上的解码时间耗在 1～2 微秒的胶水算子上，模型只以 57 tok/s「爬行」。这个数字与 orenoa7 在 RTX 5090 上测得的约 7,370 次几乎一致，两份独立测量从两个方向指向同一瓶颈。 maya-ik2（基于 @PeasantSmith 的 Project Maya 构建）的主要改动有三项：3,072 个专家全部常驻显存（共 14.7 GiB），回答期间不再从内存或磁盘读取；整段计算重放进单个 CUDA 图（CUDA Graph），把每 token 约 7,350 次启动压到 781 次（README 当前写作 757 次）；自写 Tensor Core 内核，FP8 KV（键值缓存）attention 达 776 GB/s，NVFP4 专家内核在寄存器里把 4-bit 权重即时解包成 FP16、喂给 FP16 Tensor Core（745 GB/s），因为 RTX 3090 没有 FP4 硬件。BF16 视觉编码器挪到 CPU（处理新图像 4.5 秒、缓存命中 0.5 秒），腾出的 1.3 GB 显存换来 344K 上下文容量。 他的成绩单：短上下文解码 128.7 tok/s（HTTP 服务口径 129.5）对 llama.cpp 的 57.0；4K 输入解码 124.2、prefill 2,742 items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.27962 (cs) [Submitted on 20 Nov 2026] Title: Model Carving: Training Transformers That Optimize Their Own Topology Authors: Kaden Zheng , Pratyusha Sharma View a PDF of the paper titled Model Carving: Training Transformers That Optimize Their Own Topology, by Kaden Zheng and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Machine learning has largely kept separate the choice of architecture and the process of training. A classic Transformer, for instance, trains a fixed set of attention and MLP sublayers at every layer, in the same order, and optimizes the weights within. This uniformity is a convention rather than a principled design choice, and it is likely suboptimal: the best architecture for a given task may be smaller, more efficient, and far from uniform. We believe that, ideally, training itself should shape the model's topology. To this end, we introduce Model Carving, which learns both a Transformer's weights and its architecture in a single run. By applying learnable, scalar gates to each sublayer, we allow the training loss to remove the model's own components during training -- freeing a smaller heterogeneous network inside. We evaluate Model Carving by pre-training standard Transformers from 140M to 2.7B parameters and looped Transformers from 140M to 1.3B. At equal training compute, carved models reach a lower validation loss than dense models trained with up to 1.7 times more compute. Furthermore, carved models also outperform size-matched models produced by pruning or distillation, suggesting that the best way to obtain small models for edge devices is to carve them during training, not to compress a large one afterwards. This advantage both grows with scale and carries over to downstream tasks such as few-shot evaluation and generation. Because the removed sublayers no longer run, carved models also cost up to 34% fewer FLOPs per token and decode up to 1.6 times faster without cost in quality. Our results show that architecture, like weights, should be learned and not fixed in advance, and that inside every large transformer is a smaller, faster, stronger one waiting to be carved out. Comments: 38 pages, 15 figures, 19 tables. Under review at ICLR 2027. Our results show that architecture, like weights, should be learned and not fixed in advance, and that inside every large transformer is a smaller, faster, stronger one waiting to be carved out. 1 Introduction A long-standing north star for many in machine learning has been to build models as adaptive as the brain. One field that has emerged to pursue this has been adaptive computation , which enables models to make their computations input-dependent at inference-time through techniques such as routing ( Raposo et al., 2024 ; Bae et al., 2025 ) , Mixture-of-Experts ( Shazeer et al., 2017 ) , and early-exiting ( Graves, 2016 ; Schuster et al., 2022 ) . However, among the brain’s most striking forms of plasticity is structural. During development, our brains significantly overproduce synapses and then gradually prune those whose metabolic cost outweighs their functional utility ( Huttenlocher, 1979 ; Chechik et al., 1998 ; Bullmore and Sporns, 2012 ) . Training optimizes a model’s weights within an architecture fixed before the first gradient step is taken: a classic Transformer ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) executes a homogeneous set of attention and MLP matrices at every layer, in the same fixed order. Rather than selecting an architecture and then training it, we take an overparameterized network and leverage gates to allow the training loss to remove its own components– freeing a smaller, heterogeneous network from inside (Figure 1 ). Each sublayer writes to the residual stream through a learned, scalar gate, and every sublayer that stays in the graph carries a pressure . We construct this pressure online as the loss that that sublayer’s compute would buy if spent as extra training tokens. When a sublayer contributes less to the loss than its pressure, its gate shrinks to zero and is subsequently removed from the computation graph. Therefore, by construction, a sublayer is kept only if its contribution to the loss is worth its compute. Gates and weights are optimized jointly, on the same objective, the same data, and in the same run. In this sense, we enable the architecture that performs the computation to be shaped in part by its own use. The looped Transformers are Fully Looped Transformers ( Fu et al., 2026 ) , looped four times. Each loop restarts the residual stream from the normalized token embeddings and, from the second loop on, every attention sublayer takes its queries from the previous loop’s normalized output to stabilize a known residual-norm explosion with standard looped Transformers. At each size, the two types share the width, the number of layers and heads (24 layers of width 2,048 with 32 heads at 1.3B), rotary position encoding and 4 × 4\times MLPs. We provide the shapes of every size in Appendix A . Baselines Each Model Carving run compares against two standard model baselines, trained on the same data, the same recipe, and with the same training FLOPs: (1) a “full-depth” baseline from which the carved run starts, and (2) a “shallower-depth” baseline with fewer layers to match the inference FLOPs per token of the final carved model. items.content: Ranking-Preserving Coreset Selection for Efficient Evolutionary Hyperparameter Optimization Journal: Expert Systems with Applications Mamoona Tasadduq Email: l217809@lhr.nu.edu.pk Corresponding author: Corresponding author Address: National University of Computer and Emerging Sciences (FAST-NUCES), Lahore, Pakistan Maryam Bashir Email: maryam.bashir@nu.edu.pk Address: National University of Computer and Emerging Sciences (FAST-NUCES), Lahore, Pakistan Abstract Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) is essential for achieving high predictive performance, but its computational cost becomes prohibitive when each candidate configuration requires repeated model training on large datasets. This paper proposes a ranking-preserving coreset (RPC) selection framework for accelerating evolutionary HPO. Instead of selecting instances only to preserve predictive accuracy, the proposed method constructs a compact coreset that preserves the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations observed on the full training data. Coreset selection is formulated as an evolutionary optimization problem that maximizes Spearman rank correlation between full-data and subset-based configuration rankings while penalizing subset size. The selected coreset is subsequently used for hyperparameter optimization with three evolutionary algorithms: Genetic Algorithm (GA), Cross-generational elitist Selection, Heterogeneous Recombination and Cataclysmic Mutation (CHC), and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). Extensive experiments on seven tabular, two text, and two image benchmark datasets show that the proposed framework substantially reduces HPO time while maintaining test accuracy comparable to full-dataset HPO across Decision Tree, text classification, and image classification tasks. Across datasets and optimizers, the proposed method achieves HPO stage speedups ranging approximately from 1.14 × 1.14\times to 8.80 × 8.80\times , while the one-time coreset construction cost is accounted for separately through end-to-end runtime and break-even analysis. On 20 held-out configurations not used during coreset construction, RPC achieved higher ranking correlation than same-size random sampling on 8 of 11 datasets (dataset-level Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.014 p=0.014 ). This demonstrates that ranking preservation extends beyond the configurations used during selection. Coreset construction incurs a one-time cost, which can be amortized when the coreset is reused across HPO runs. Keywords: Hyperparameter Optimization, Coreset Selection, Evolutionary Algorithms, Machine Learning, Ranking Preservation, Computational Efficiency 1 Introduction Machine learning has revolutionized our ability to extract meaningful insights from vast and diverse datasets across a wide range of application domains. Among its various paradigms, deep learning has gained significant attention for its ability to automatically learn hierarchical representations from data. Machine learning and deep learning models have demonstrated remarkable success in areas such as classification, prediction, computer vision, and natural language processing. However, training and optimizing these models often require substantial computational resources, particularly when dealing with large, high-dimensional datasets. The selection of hyperparameters often influences model performance and accuracy [ Rimal et al., 2024 ] . Depending on the learning algorithm, these may include parameters such as learning rate, batch size, optimizer settings, tree depth, network architecture, splitting criteria, and regularization parameters. Identifying suitable hyperparameter configurations is essential for achieving optimal predictive performance. Nevertheless, balancing computational efficiency and model performance remains a significant challenge, especially when the size, complexity, and dimensionality of modern datasets continue to grow. The computational burden of training and optimizing machine learning and deep learning models can be reduced through techniques such as instance selection, feature selection, and efficient hyperparameter optimization [ Dhanka et al., 2026 , Yu et al., 2024 ] . Among these, instance selection aims to identify a representative subset of instances from the original dataset while preserving its essential characteristics. Instance selection has proven effective at reducing computational costs by decreasing the amount of data processed during model training and evaluation [ Guo et al., 2022 ] . In addition, hyperparameter optimization seeks to identify the combination of hyperparameter values within a predefined search space that yields the best predictive performance [ Ali et al., 2023 ] . However, repeatedly evaluating numerous hyperparameter configurations remains computationally expensive, particularly for large-scale and high-dimensional datasets. Hyperparameter optimization has become a fundamental component of modern machine learning pipelines, as model performance is often highly sensitive to hyperparameter choices [ Rimal et al., 2024 ] . While traditional hyperparameter optimization techniques such as Grid Search and Random Search are valued for their straightforward implementation, they scale poorly and suffer from prohibitive computational overhead as the dimensionality of the search space increases [ Bergstra and Bengio, 2012 , Belete and Huchaiah, 2022 , Ali et al., 2023 ] . To mitigate these computational bottlenecks, more sophisticated sequential methodologies, such as Bayesian Optimization, Hyperband, and metaheuristic evolutionary algorithms, have been proposed to improve search efficiency while reducing the number of costly model evaluations [ Klein et al., 2017 , Lorenzo et al., 2017 , Srinivas and Katarya, 2022 ] . Consequently, modern frameworks like Optuna have been deployed to optimize complex architectures, such as tuning an XGBoost classifier for cardiovascular disease prediction, without the computational overhead of traditional search methods [ Srinivas and Katarya, 2022 ] . Despite these advances, the repeated training and evaluation of models across numerous candidate configurations remain a major computational bottleneck, particularly for large-scale datasets and deep learning applications. For instance, training 10 candidates over 10 generations entails approximately 100 model training runs per HPO run. Repeated search across multiple optimizers and seeds can multiply this cost, particularly when using the full training dataset. Coreset construction incurs an upfront overhead; therefore, its overall runtime benefit only comes when the time saved across HPO runs exceeds the time spent constructing the coreset. Recent advances in dataset reduction and coreset selection have demonstrated that carefully selected subsets can substantially reduce the computational cost of model training while preserving predictive performance [ Guo et al., 2022 ] . Gradient-based approaches such as GLISTER [ Killamsetty et al., 2021b ] and GRAD-MATCH [ Killamsetty et al., 2021a ] select training subsets by optimizing validation performance and matching full-data gradients, respectively, whereas more recent methods have explored clustering-based [ Saha et al., 2022 ] , bi-level optimization [ Zhou et al., 2022 ] , and submodular [ Wei et al., 2015 ] strategies for efficient data selection in both conventional machine learning and large-scale language models. Despite their effectiveness in reducing training costs, these approaches primarily focus on preserving model performance and training dynamics rather than preserving the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations. Consequently, a subset that performs well during model training may not preserve the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations needed for reliable hyperparameter optimization. This limitation motivates the development of ranking-aware data-reduction strategies specifically designed to accelerate hyperparameter optimization. Ranking-aware surrogate methods have investigated relative configuration ordering as an alternative to predicting exact performance values. For instance, Khazi et al. [2023] proposed Deep Ranking Ensembles, which use ranking-based surrogate models to guide HPO by prioritizing the relative ordering of candidate configurations rather than precise performance predictions. This motivates investigating ranking agreement as a criterion for training-subset selection. Whereas Deep Ranking Ensembles learn a surrogate to guide configuration selection, RPC selects the training instances used to evaluate configurations. Ranking preservation is relevant to evolutionary HPO because selection decisions often depend on the relative performance of candidate configurations. If a subset preserves their ordering, rank-based decisions, such as tournament selection and elite retention, can remain unchanged despite differences in absolute validation scores. However, ranking agreement on reference configurations does not guarantee an identical search trajectory or final predictive performance: unseen configurations, ties, and decision rules involving score magnitudes can still affect the search. Motivated by these considerations, we propose a ranking-preserving coreset framework that optimizes agreement between full-data and subset-induced hyperparameter rankings over reference configurations while penalizing subset size. Unlike conventional instance selection and coreset methods that focus primarily on preserving predictive accuracy or training dynamics, the proposed method preserves the configuration ranking structure that guides evolutionary HPO algorithms, enabling them to identify promising regions of the search space without requiring exact replication of full-dataset validation accuracies. This makes the proposed framework suitable for repeated model-selection workflows, where high-quality configurations must be identified with fewer evaluations on the full training dataset. Based on the identified research gap, this study addresses the following research questions: • RQ1: Can a compact ranking-preserving coreset maintain predictive performance close to full-dataset hyperparameter optimization while using substantially fewer training instances? • RQ2: How effectively does the proposed coreset preserve the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations compared with same-size random and gradient-based subsets? • RQ3: Does the ranking preservation achieved during coreset construction generalize to unseen held-out hyperparameter configurations? • RQ4: Under what conditions does the proposed framework provide computational savings after accounting for the one-time coreset construction cost? Main Contributions The primary contributions of this work are summarized as follows: 1. Ranking-Preserving Coreset Selection Framework: We propose a ranking-preserving coreset selection framework that constructs compact training subsets specifically designed to preserve the relative performance ordering of hyperparameter configurations observed on the full training dataset. 2. Evolutionary Ranking-Aware Optimization Objective: We formulate coreset selection as an evolutionary optimization problem that jointly maximizes ranking fidelity, measured using Spearman rank correlation, and penalizes subset size. This enables the construction of compact coresets that preserve the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations. 3. Efficient Evolutionary Hyperparameter Optimization: We integrate the selected coreset into evolutionary HPO, allowing GA, CHC, and PSO to search for high-quality hyperparameter configurations using substantially fewer training instances while maintaining performance close to that of full-dataset HPO. 4. Comprehensive Multi-Modal Evaluation: We evaluate the proposed framework across 11 benchmark datasets, including seven UCI tabular datasets, two text datasets (IMDb and TweetEval Sentiment), and two image datasets (CIFAR-10 and DermaMNIST). The evaluation covers Decision Trees for tabular data, TF-IDF with a PyTorch MLP for text classification, and ResNet18 for image classification. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the literature on instance selection, coreset construction, and hyperparameter optimization. Section 3 presents the proposed ranking-preserving coreset selection framework and the evolutionary optimization strategy. Section 4 describes the experimental setup. Section 5 reports and discusses the results obtained on UCI tabular datasets, text classification datasets, and image classification datasets. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future research. 2 Related Work In this section, we present a comprehensive review of the latest studies related to instance selection, coreset construction, hyperparameter optimization, and evolutionary search. The aim is to explore the methods that reduce computational cost through representative data selection and efficient hyperparameter exploration, as these areas are most closely related to the proposed ranking-preserving coreset selection framework. Instance selection aims to identify a representative subset of data instances that preserves the essential characteristics of the original dataset while reducing computational cost. Because subset selection can be formulated as a search problem, evolutionary and metaheuristic approaches have been widely investigated for this purpose. Various studies have explored the potential of using evolutionary algorithms for instance selection in different domains. Tsai et al. [2013] investigated the potential of genetic algorithms for instance and feature selection in knowledge-based systems to enhance computational efficiency. Another paper authored by Kordos et al. [2022] proposes a framework that uses fuzzy clustering decomposition in combination with a genetic algorithm. The framework uses fuzzy clustering to decompose the dataset into coherent clusters and selects the representative instances from these clusters to perform regression tasks. The authors underscore the effectiveness of this hybrid model for high-dimensional data in improving model performance and generalization for regression problems. The study conducted by Onan and Korukoğlu [2016] evaluates the effectiveness of fifteen instance selection methods within the domain of text sentiment classification. The authors highlight the performance of different instance selection methods for data reduction, providing insights into the appropriate selection of an instance selection technique for text sentiment analysis. Rathee et al. [2018] proposed a Multi-Objective CHC evolutionary algorithm for instance selection that integrates the non-dominated sorting with CHC. The proposed algorithm demonstrated 50% reduction in the dataset while not compromising data accuracy for most of the dataset when compared with KNN. Recent advances in coreset construction have further demonstrated the effectiveness of selecting representative subsets in reducing computational cost while preserving model performance. Gradient-based approaches such as GRAD-MATCH [ Killamsetty et al., 2021a ] and GLISTER [ Killamsetty et al., 2021b ] construct representative subsets by matching gradient information or optimizing validation performance through bilevel optimization. Other studies have explored clustering-based [ Saha et al., 2022 ] , submodular [ Wei et al., 2015 ] , and bilevel optimization strategies [ Zhou et al., 2022 ] for efficient data reduction in both conventional machine learning and large-scale language models. In parallel, recent work by Khazi et al. [2023] highlighted the importance of preserving the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations during optimization, demonstrating that ranking-aware surrogate models can effectively guide hyperparameter search without requiring highly accurate performance prediction. While these studies illustrate the importance of both representative data selection and ranking preservation, they have largely been investigated independently. The methods compared in Table 1 differ in their optimization targets: existing subset-selection methods emphasize gradients, validation performance, or data representativeness, whereas ranking-aware surrogates guide configuration selection. RPC instead directly optimizes configuration-ranking agreement during training-subset selection. In the literature, many studies have explored the importance and techniques of hyperparameter tuning for deep learning tasks. The use of genetic algorithms for HPO has gained significant attention in the domain of machine learning and optimization. Researchers have explored the potential of GAs to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of hyperparameter optimization. However, a comparative study conducted by Alibrahim and Ludwig [2021] highlights the strengths and limitations of three hyperparameter techniques, i.e., Bayesian, grid, and GA. The authors conducted empirical evaluations and provided insights into the trade-offs and capabilities of each optimization method for a particular scenario. Evolutionary HPO studies provide methodological context for the GA and PSO optimizers evaluated in this work. They investigate how evolutionary search identifies promising hyperparameter configurations, while RPC addresses the training-data cost of evaluating those configurations. Erden [2023] demonstrated the applicability of GAs in HPO for deep learning models in the context of PM2.5 time-series prediction, emphasizing their potential in improving predictive accuracy. It showed promising results when compared with default hyperparameters and random search algorithms for air quality forecasting. The proposed HPO outperformed other methods by significantly reducing the MSE. Additionally, Tani et al. [2021] demonstrated the use of PSO and GA to select an optimal set of hyperparameters for machine learning models used in high-energy physics data analysis, achieving significantly improved sensitivity (by 12-13%) compared with the default hyperparameter settings. The results of another study showed the effectiveness of GA in optimizing hyperparameters for predictive business process monitoring [ Di Francescomarino et al., 2018 ] . Altarabichi et al. [2023] proposed a qualitative approximation approach for feature selection using a genetic algorithm. This study aims to identify the best feature subset from the complex dataset more efficiently, thereby offering a lightweight model to enhance performance. Lee et al. [2021] leverage GA to jointly optimize a neural network’s architecture, such as the number of neurons and layers, and hyperparameters, such as the learning rate and batch size. The empirical results of the study demonstrate effectiveness in performance, thereby providing insights for enhancing the capabilities of deep learning models. Hyperparameter optimization is equally important in deep CNNs, where complex, high-dimensional data, particularly images, are used for analysis and insight generation. Aszemi and Dominic [2019] addresses the challenges of hyperparameter tuning to enhance the performance of image-related tasks. The authors explored a genetic algorithm-based approach to enhance the performance of convolutional neural networks. items.raw_text: Ranking-Preserving Coreset Selection for Efficient Evolutionary Hyperparameter Optimization Journal: Expert Systems with Applications Mamoona Tasadduq Email: l217809@lhr.nu.edu.pk Corresponding author: Corresponding author Address: National University of Computer and Emerging Sciences (FAST-NUCES), Lahore, Pakistan Maryam Bashir Email: maryam.bashir@nu.edu.pk Address: National University of Computer and Emerging Sciences (FAST-NUCES), Lahore, Pakistan Abstract Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) is essential for achieving high predictive performance, but its computational cost becomes prohibitive when each candidate configuration requires repeated model training on large datasets. This paper proposes a ranking-preserving coreset (RPC) selection framework for accelerating evolutionary HPO. Instead of selecting instances only to preserve predictive accuracy, the proposed method constructs a compact coreset that preserves the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations observed on the full training data. Coreset selection is formulated as an evolutionary optimization problem that maximizes Spearman rank correlation between full-data and subset-based configuration rankings while penalizing subset size. The selected coreset is subsequently used for hyperparameter optimization with three evolutionary algorithms: Genetic Algorithm (GA), Cross-generational elitist Selection, Heterogeneous Recombination and Cataclysmic Mutation (CHC), and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). Extensive experiments on seven tabular, two text, and two image benchmark datasets show that the proposed framework substantially reduces HPO time while maintaining test accuracy comparable to full-dataset HPO across Decision Tree, text classification, and image classification tasks. Across datasets and optimizers, the proposed method achieves HPO stage speedups ranging approximately from 1.14 × 1.14\times to 8.80 × 8.80\times , while the one-time coreset construction cost is accounted for separately through end-to-end runtime and break-even analysis. On 20 held-out configurations not used during coreset construction, RPC achieved higher ranking correlation than same-size random sampling on 8 of 11 datasets (dataset-level Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.014 p=0.014 ). This demonstrates that ranking preservation extends beyond the configurations used during selection. Coreset construction incurs a one-time cost, which can be amortized when the coreset is reused across HPO runs. Keywords: Hyperparameter Optimization, Coreset Selection, Evolutionary Algorithms, Machine Learning, Ranking Preservation, Computational Efficiency 1 Introduction Machine learning has revolutionized our ability to extract meaningful insights from vast and diverse datasets across a wide range of application domains. Among its various paradigms, deep learning has gained significant attention for its ability to automatically learn hierarchical representations from data. Machine learning and deep learning models have demonstrated remarkable success in areas such as classification, prediction, computer vision, and natural language processing. However, training and optimizing these models often require substantial computational resources, particularly when dealing with large, high-dimensional datasets. The selection of hyperparameters often influences model performance and accuracy [ Rimal et al., 2024 ] . Depending on the learning algorithm, these may include parameters such as learning rate, batch size, optimizer settings, tree depth, network architecture, splitting criteria, and regularization parameters. Identifying suitable hyperparameter configurations is essential for achieving optimal predictive performance. Nevertheless, balancing computational efficiency and model performance remains a significant challenge, especially when the size, complexity, and dimensionality of modern datasets continue to grow. The computational burden of training and optimizing machine learning and deep learning models can be reduced through techniques such as instance selection, feature selection, and efficient hyperparameter optimization [ Dhanka et al., 2026 , Yu et al., 2024 ] . Among these, instance selection aims to identify a representative subset of instances from the original dataset while preserving its essential characteristics. Instance selection has proven effective at reducing computational costs by decreasing the amount of data processed during model training and evaluation [ Guo et al., 2022 ] . In addition, hyperparameter optimization seeks to identify the combination of hyperparameter values within a predefined search space that yields the best predictive performance [ Ali et al., 2023 ] . However, repeatedly evaluating numerous hyperparameter configurations remains computationally expensive, particularly for large-scale and high-dimensional datasets. Hyperparameter optimization has become a fundamental component of modern machine learning pipelines, as model performance is often highly sensitive to hyperparameter choices [ Rimal et al., 2024 ] . While traditional hyperparameter optimization techniques such as Grid Search and Random Search are valued for their straightforward implementation, they scale poorly and suffer from prohibitive computational overhead as the dimensionality of the search space increases [ Bergstra and Bengio, 2012 , Belete and Huchaiah, 2022 , Ali et al., 2023 ] . To mitigate these computational bottlenecks, more sophisticated sequential methodologies, such as Bayesian Optimization, Hyperband, and metaheuristic evolutionary algorithms, have been proposed to improve search efficiency while reducing the number of costly model evaluations [ Klein et al., 2017 , Lorenzo et al., 2017 , Srinivas and Katarya, 2022 ] . Consequently, modern frameworks like Optuna have been deployed to optimize complex architectures, such as tuning an XGBoost classifier for cardiovascular disease prediction, without the computational overhead of traditional search methods [ Srinivas and Katarya, 2022 ] . Despite these advances, the repeated training and evaluation of models across numerous candidate configurations remain a major computational bottleneck, particularly for large-scale datasets and deep learning applications. For instance, training 10 candidates over 10 generations entails approximately 100 model training runs per HPO run. Repeated search across multiple optimizers and seeds can multiply this cost, particularly when using the full training dataset. Coreset construction incurs an upfront overhead; therefore, its overall runtime benefit only comes when the time saved across HPO runs exceeds the time spent constructing the coreset. Recent advances in dataset reduction and coreset selection have demonstrated that carefully selected subsets can substantially reduce the computational cost of model training while preserving predictive performance [ Guo et al., 2022 ] . Gradient-based approaches such as GLISTER [ Killamsetty et al., 2021b ] and GRAD-MATCH [ Killamsetty et al., 2021a ] select training subsets by optimizing validation performance and matching full-data gradients, respectively, whereas more recent methods have explored clustering-based [ Saha et al., 2022 ] , bi-level optimization [ Zhou et al., 2022 ] , and submodular [ Wei et al., 2015 ] strategies for efficient data selection in both conventional machine learning and large-scale language models. Despite their effectiveness in reducing training costs, these approaches primarily focus on preserving model performance and training dynamics rather than preserving the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations. Consequently, a subset that performs well during model training may not preserve the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations needed for reliable hyperparameter optimization. This limitation motivates the development of ranking-aware data-reduction strategies specifically designed to accelerate hyperparameter optimization. Ranking-aware surrogate methods have investigated relative configuration ordering as an alternative to predicting exact performance values. For instance, Khazi et al. [2023] proposed Deep Ranking Ensembles, which use ranking-based surrogate models to guide HPO by prioritizing the relative ordering of candidate configurations rather than precise performance predictions. This motivates investigating ranking agreement as a criterion for training-subset selection. Whereas Deep Ranking Ensembles learn a surrogate to guide configuration selection, RPC selects the training instances used to evaluate configurations. Ranking preservation is relevant to evolutionary HPO because selection decisions often depend on the relative performance of candidate configurations. If a subset preserves their ordering, rank-based decisions, such as tournament selection and elite retention, can remain unchanged despite differences in absolute validation scores. However, ranking agreement on reference configurations does not guarantee an identical search trajectory or final predictive performance: unseen configurations, ties, and decision rules involving score magnitudes can still affect the search. Motivated by these considerations, we propose a ranking-preserving coreset framework that optimizes agreement between full-data and subset-induced hyperparameter rankings over reference configurations while penalizing subset size. Unlike conventional instance selection and coreset methods that focus primarily on preserving predictive accuracy or training dynamics, the proposed method preserves the configuration ranking structure that guides evolutionary HPO algorithms, enabling them to identify promising regions of the search space without requiring exact replication of full-dataset validation accuracies. This makes the proposed framework suitable for repeated model-selection workflows, where high-quality configurations must be identified with fewer evaluations on the full training dataset. Based on the identified research gap, this study addresses the following research questions: • RQ1: Can a compact ranking-preserving coreset maintain predictive performance close to full-dataset hyperparameter optimization while using substantially fewer training instances? • RQ2: How effectively does the proposed coreset preserve the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations compared with same-size random and gradient-based subsets? • RQ3: Does the ranking preservation achieved during coreset construction generalize to unseen held-out hyperparameter configurations? • RQ4: Under what conditions does the proposed framework provide computational savings after accounting for the one-time coreset construction cost? Main Contributions The primary contributions of this work are summarized as follows: 1. Ranking-Preserving Coreset Selection Framework: We propose a ranking-preserving coreset selection framework that constructs compact training subsets specifically designed to preserve the relative performance ordering of hyperparameter configurations observed on the full training dataset. 2. Evolutionary Ranking-Aware Optimization Objective: We formulate coreset selection as an evolutionary optimization problem that jointly maximizes ranking fidelity, measured using Spearman rank correlation, and penalizes subset size. This enables the construction of compact coresets that preserve the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations. 3. Efficient Evolutionary Hyperparameter Optimization: We integrate the selected coreset into evolutionary HPO, allowing GA, CHC, and PSO to search for high-quality hyperparameter configurations using substantially fewer training instances while maintaining performance close to that of full-dataset HPO. 4. Comprehensive Multi-Modal Evaluation: We evaluate the proposed framework across 11 benchmark datasets, including seven UCI tabular datasets, two text datasets (IMDb and TweetEval Sentiment), and two image datasets (CIFAR-10 and DermaMNIST). The evaluation covers Decision Trees for tabular data, TF-IDF with a PyTorch MLP for text classification, and ResNet18 for image classification. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the literature on instance selection, coreset construction, and hyperparameter optimization. Section 3 presents the proposed ranking-preserving coreset selection framework and the evolutionary optimization strategy. Section 4 describes the experimental setup. Section 5 reports and discusses the results obtained on UCI tabular datasets, text classification datasets, and image classification datasets. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future research. 2 Related Work In this section, we present a comprehensive review of the latest studies related to instance selection, coreset construction, hyperparameter optimization, and evolutionary search. The aim is to explore the methods that reduce computational cost through representative data selection and efficient hyperparameter exploration, as these areas are most closely related to the proposed ranking-preserving coreset selection framework. Instance selection aims to identify a representative subset of data instances that preserves the essential characteristics of the original dataset while reducing computational cost. Because subset selection can be formulated as a search problem, evolutionary and metaheuristic approaches have been widely investigated for this purpose. Various studies have explored the potential of using evolutionary algorithms for instance selection in different domains. Tsai et al. [2013] investigated the potential of genetic algorithms for instance and feature selection in knowledge-based systems to enhance computational efficiency. Another paper authored by Kordos et al. [2022] proposes a framework that uses fuzzy clustering decomposition in combination with a genetic algorithm. The framework uses fuzzy clustering to decompose the dataset into coherent clusters and selects the representative instances from these clusters to perform regression tasks. The authors underscore the effectiveness of this hybrid model for high-dimensional data in improving model performance and generalization for regression problems. The study conducted by Onan and Korukoğlu [2016] evaluates the effectiveness of fifteen instance selection methods within the domain of text sentiment classification. The authors highlight the performance of different instance selection methods for data reduction, providing insights into the appropriate selection of an instance selection technique for text sentiment analysis. Rathee et al. [2018] proposed a Multi-Objective CHC evolutionary algorithm for instance selection that integrates the non-dominated sorting with CHC. The proposed algorithm demonstrated 50% reduction in the dataset while not compromising data accuracy for most of the dataset when compared with KNN. Recent advances in coreset construction have further demonstrated the effectiveness of selecting representative subsets in reducing computational cost while preserving model performance. Gradient-based approaches such as GRAD-MATCH [ Killamsetty et al., 2021a ] and GLISTER [ Killamsetty et al., 2021b ] construct representative subsets by matching gradient information or optimizing validation performance through bilevel optimization. Other studies have explored clustering-based [ Saha et al., 2022 ] , submodular [ Wei et al., 2015 ] , and bilevel optimization strategies [ Zhou et al., 2022 ] for efficient data reduction in both conventional machine learning and large-scale language models. In parallel, recent work by Khazi et al. [2023] highlighted the importance of preserving the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations during optimization, demonstrating that ranking-aware surrogate models can effectively guide hyperparameter search without requiring highly accurate performance prediction. RPC instead directly optimizes configuration-ranking agreement during training-subset selection. Researchers have explored the potential of GAs to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of hyperparameter optimization. However, a comparative study conducted by Alibrahim and Ludwig [2021] highlights the strengths and limitations of three hyperparameter techniques, i.e., Bayesian, grid, and GA. The authors conducted empirical evaluations and provided insights into the trade-offs and capabilities of each optimization method for a particular scenario. items.content: Functional Depth Is Learned: Isolating the Computation That Layers Produce Only Together JaeSeong Kim † † thanks: Work done during an internship at MLP Lab, KAIST. KyungTae Lim † † thanks: Corresponding author. Abstract Transformer performance scales with depth, but layer count merely counts the opportunities for sequential computation: layers could still behave as nearly independent refinements that barely depend on one another. We study how transformers develop functional depth during pretraining, introducing an exact inclusion–exclusion decomposition that isolates the connected component—the computation that appears only when a specified set of layers acts together under identity ablation. Tracking this quantity across public checkpoints of Pythia, OLMo, and Amber yields three findings. First, write-relative connected coordination strengthens from its initialization or earliest-checkpoint baseline as pretraining proceeds, across all measured interaction orders. Second, these connected components are behaviorally consequential under direct intervention: deleting them damages perplexity more than deleting a norm-matched random direction at the same site in all 35 measured model–order cells. Third, pairwise representation similarity is consistently negatively correlated with pairwise connected coordination across seven models, yet the two signals are not interchangeable: similarity- and coordination-based block-removal criteria often agree in Pythia but diverge on Amber. Together, these results suggest that architectural depth provides the opportunity for sequential computation, while pretraining progressively organizes cross-layer dependencies within that depth. 1 Semyung University, Jecheon-si, Republic of Korea 2 Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology kjsqp1010@semyung.ac.kr, ktlim@kaist.ac.kr 1 Introduction Depth is one of the few reliable scaling axes of modern transformers, and recent studies have shown that stacking layers is central to improving model performance ( Kaplan et al. 2020 ; Tay et al. 2022 ; Petty et al. 2024 ) . Unfortunately, the mechanism behind what added depth actually buys remains poorly understood. A stacked architecture offers as many opportunities for sequential computation as it has layers, yet a trained model could still behave as a collection of nearly independent refinements ( Veit et al. 2016 ; Jastrzębski et al. 2018 ) , with each layer editing the residual stream ( Elhage et al. 2021 ) without depending on combinations of earlier computations. Architectural depth, in other words, is only potential depth. Existing analysis tools—representation similarity ( Raghu et al. 2017 ; Kornblith et al. 2019 ; Nguyen et al. 2021 ) , layer lenses ( Belrose et al. 2023 ) , and layer-skipping and reordering studies ( Freiberger et al. 2024 ; Sun et al. 2025 ) —inspect layers individually or in pairs; they can measure what each layer leaves behind, but not the computation that multiple layers produce only when present together. In this work, we take an initial step toward understanding the dynamics by which functional depth is formed during transformer pretraining. We investigate three important research questions that remain unanswered: RQ1. Do the layers of a trained transformer actually compute jointly across depth, or do they behave as a stack of independent refinements? And how does this cross-layer coupling structure change over the course of pretraining? RQ2. Is the computation that layers produce only together behaviorally consequential under direct intervention, relative to an equal-norm perturbation at the same site? RQ3. Does cross-layer connective structure provide a complementary account of the phenomena reported by layerwise and pairwise analyses? Figure 1: Development of connected cross-layer coordination during pretraining (pythia-410m). Each panel visualizes one checkpoint (columns, init–64k steps) at one interaction order k k (rows, k = 3 k=3 – 6 6 ): nodes are layers ordered by depth, and each arc spans an adjacent window T T of k k layers, with intensity proportional to its normalized connected component U ^ T \widehat{U}_{T} , scaled by the order-level ratio R k R_{k} . Coordination is weak relative to later checkpoints at initialization and progressively concentrates into an early-interior band as training proceeds, across every measured order. Our experiments reveal several important insights into the fine-grained dynamics by which functional depth is formed during transformer pretraining. First, we find that functional depth, operationalized by write-relative connected components, strengthens during pretraining (Figure 1 ). At initialization or at the earliest released checkpoints ( Biderman et al. 2023 ; Groeneveld et al. 2024 ) , normalized connected components are substantially smaller, particularly at higher interaction orders, whereas later checkpoints exhibit larger connected components across all measured orders and depths. Our normalization expresses each connected component relative to the actual write of the final participating layer, allowing us to compare interaction strength against a local write scale rather than raw residual magnitude. The resulting pattern is consistent with pretraining progressively organizing cross-layer interactions across depth. Second, the connected component is causally load-bearing rather than an algebraic remainder. Deleting it damages perplexity more than deleting a norm-matched random direction of the same size at the same site, in all 35 of our measured model–order cells, with the gap exceeding two orders of magnitude in the largest models. Third, representation similarity is systematically associated with weak cross-layer coordination, while the two quantities remain distinct. Across seven models differing in scale and training data, pairwise similarity is consistently negatively correlated with the normalized connected component, so layer pairs with more similar representations tend to exhibit weaker pairwise connected computation. Taken together, to the best of our knowledge, this work is among the first attempts to isolate cross-layer joint computation in transformers with an exact estimand and to trace its development. Layer count specifies only the possibility of depth; whether that possibility becomes an organized computation is decided by pretraining. By treating functional depth as an empirical property of a trained computation rather than an architectural hyperparameter, we hope to help the community build a holistic understanding of deep models and make better-informed decisions about pruning, compression, and scaling. 2 Related Work Most analyses of transformer depth build on the residual-stream view of each block as an identity map plus a per-layer update ( Elhage et al. 2021 ) , and inspect one or two layers at a time: decoding the state at each layer ( nostalgebraist 2020 ; Belrose et al. 2023 ) , comparing pairs of representations ( Raghu et al. 2017 ; Kornblith et al. 2019 ; Nguyen et al. 2021 ) , or scoring single blocks for skipping, reordering, or pruning ( Freiberger et al. 2024 ; Sun et al. 2025 ; Gromov et al. 2025 ; Men et al. 2024 ) . Causal-intervention methods likewise localize behavior by patching activations at chosen sites ( Meng et al. 2022 ; Wang et al. 2023 ; Goldowsky-Dill et al. 2023 ; Chan et al. 2022 ; Zhang and Nanda 2024 ) ; the cross-layer attribution methods of Lindsey et al. (2024) , Dunefsky et al. (2024) , and Lindsey et al. (2025) are closest in spirit, but decompose the representation into features spanning layers. We instead decompose the function : whether one layer’s write changes how later layers compute, including effects requiring three or more layers jointly, with the residual identity as the null—the only value under which U T U_{T} vanishes exactly when a participating layer is removed (Section 5.3 contrasts the resulting block-removal rankings with similarity-based ones). Residual networks have been read as ensembles of shallow paths ( Veit et al. 2016 ) or as iterative inference ( Jastrzębski et al. 2018 ) ; the former enumerates subpaths, whereas we isolate what the full path contributes beyond every proper subpath. Formally, our estimand is the Möbius transform, or Harsanyi dividend, of the set function induced by layer ablation ( Harsanyi 1963 ; Grabisch and Roubens 1999 ) , standard for input features and tokens ( Sundararajan et al. 2020 ; Tsai et al. 2023 ; Hao et al. 2021 ) . We differ in that the payoff is a vector-valued residual write, the players are noncommutative maps, and the residual-identity null makes the decomposition exact; connecting to studies of training dynamics ( Nanda et al. 2023 ; Olsson et al. 2022 ; Hoogland et al. 2024 ) , we track this quantity across pretraining, asking not what a model represents but how many layers must act together before a computation exists at all. 3 Cross-Layer Coordination The number of layers the architecture supplies must be distinguished from the depth the trained model actually uses: if each layer edited the residual stream independently of the computations before it, the model would behave less like a deep computation than like a collection of independent refinements applied in sequence. We therefore define cross-layer coordination as follows. If a later layer produces the same update regardless of the outputs of earlier layers, the layers compute independently; if the results of earlier layers change what the later layer computes, the layers coordinate. Coordination is thus not several layers producing large updates, but one layer’s computation depending conditionally on the computations that precede it. Our goal is to isolate the component that appears only when a specified set of layers all act together, and that is not explained by any proper subset. 3.1 The Connected Component as Conditional Computation Consider a pretrained transformer with L L layers, and let h ( ℓ ) ∈ ℝ d h^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote the residual-stream state entering layer ℓ \ell . items.raw_text: Functional Depth Is Learned: Isolating the Computation That Layers Produce Only Together JaeSeong Kim † † thanks: Work done during an internship at MLP Lab, KAIST. KyungTae Lim † † thanks: Corresponding author. Abstract Transformer performance scales with depth, but layer count merely counts the opportunities for sequential computation: layers could still behave as nearly independent refinements that barely depend on one another. We study how transformers develop functional depth during pretraining, introducing an exact inclusion–exclusion decomposition that isolates the connected component—the computation that appears only when a specified set of layers acts together under identity ablation. Tracking this quantity across public checkpoints of Pythia, OLMo, and Amber yields three findings. First, write-relative connected coordination strengthens from its initialization or earliest-checkpoint baseline as pretraining proceeds, across all measured interaction orders. Second, these connected components are behaviorally consequential under direct intervention: deleting them damages perplexity more than deleting a norm-matched random direction at the same site in all 35 measured model–order cells. Third, pairwise representation similarity is consistently negatively correlated with pairwise connected coordination across seven models, yet the two signals are not interchangeable: similarity- and coordination-based block-removal criteria often agree in Pythia but diverge on Amber. Together, these results suggest that architectural depth provides the opportunity for sequential computation, while pretraining progressively organizes cross-layer dependencies within that depth. 1 Semyung University, Jecheon-si, Republic of Korea 2 Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology kjsqp1010@semyung.ac.kr, ktlim@kaist.ac.kr 1 Introduction Depth is one of the few reliable scaling axes of modern transformers, and recent studies have shown that stacking layers is central to improving model performance ( Kaplan et al. 2020 ; Tay et al. 2022 ; Petty et al. 2024 ) . Unfortunately, the mechanism behind what added depth actually buys remains poorly understood. A stacked architecture offers as many opportunities for sequential computation as it has layers, yet a trained model could still behave as a collection of nearly independent refinements ( Veit et al. 2016 ; Jastrzębski et al. 2018 ) , with each layer editing the residual stream ( Elhage et al. 2021 ) without depending on combinations of earlier computations. Architectural depth, in other words, is only potential depth. Existing analysis tools—representation similarity ( Raghu et al. 2017 ; Kornblith et al. 2019 ; Nguyen et al. 2021 ) , layer lenses ( Belrose et al. 2023 ) , and layer-skipping and reordering studies ( Freiberger et al. 2024 ; Sun et al. 2025 ) —inspect layers individually or in pairs; they can measure what each layer leaves behind, but not the computation that multiple layers produce only when present together. In this work, we take an initial step toward understanding the dynamics by which functional depth is formed during transformer pretraining. We investigate three important research questions that remain unanswered: RQ1. Do the layers of a trained transformer actually compute jointly across depth, or do they behave as a stack of independent refinements? And how does this cross-layer coupling structure change over the course of pretraining? RQ2. Is the computation that layers produce only together behaviorally consequential under direct intervention, relative to an equal-norm perturbation at the same site? RQ3. Does cross-layer connective structure provide a complementary account of the phenomena reported by layerwise and pairwise analyses? Figure 1: Development of connected cross-layer coordination during pretraining (pythia-410m). Each panel visualizes one checkpoint (columns, init–64k steps) at one interaction order k k (rows, k = 3 k=3 – 6 6 ): nodes are layers ordered by depth, and each arc spans an adjacent window T T of k k layers, with intensity proportional to its normalized connected component U ^ T \widehat{U}_{T} , scaled by the order-level ratio R k R_{k} . Coordination is weak relative to later checkpoints at initialization and progressively concentrates into an early-interior band as training proceeds, across every measured order. Our experiments reveal several important insights into the fine-grained dynamics by which functional depth is formed during transformer pretraining. First, we find that functional depth, operationalized by write-relative connected components, strengthens during pretraining (Figure 1 ). At initialization or at the earliest released checkpoints ( Biderman et al. 2023 ; Groeneveld et al. 2024 ) , normalized connected components are substantially smaller, particularly at higher interaction orders, whereas later checkpoints exhibit larger connected components across all measured orders and depths. Our normalization expresses each connected component relative to the actual write of the final participating layer, allowing us to compare interaction strength against a local write scale rather than raw residual magnitude. The resulting pattern is consistent with pretraining progressively organizing cross-layer interactions across depth. Second, the connected component is causally load-bearing rather than an algebraic remainder. Deleting it damages perplexity more than deleting a norm-matched random direction of the same size at the same site, in all 35 of our measured model–order cells, with the gap exceeding two orders of magnitude in the largest models. Third, representation similarity is systematically associated with weak cross-layer coordination, while the two quantities remain distinct. Across seven models differing in scale and training data, pairwise similarity is consistently negatively correlated with the normalized connected component, so layer pairs with more similar representations tend to exhibit weaker pairwise connected computation. Taken together, to the best of our knowledge, this work is among the first attempts to isolate cross-layer joint computation in transformers with an exact estimand and to trace its development. Layer count specifies only the possibility of depth; whether that possibility becomes an organized computation is decided by pretraining. By treating functional depth as an empirical property of a trained computation rather than an architectural hyperparameter, we hope to help the community build a holistic understanding of deep models and make better-informed decisions about pruning, compression, and scaling. 2 Related Work Most analyses of transformer depth build on the residual-stream view of each block as an identity map plus a per-layer update ( Elhage et al. 2021 ) , and inspect one or two layers at a time: decoding the state at each layer ( nostalgebraist 2020 ; Belrose et al. 2023 ) , comparing pairs of representations ( Raghu et al. 2017 ; Kornblith et al. 2019 ; Nguyen et al. 2021 ) , or scoring single blocks for skipping, reordering, or pruning ( Freiberger et al. 2024 ; Sun et al. 2025 ; Gromov et al. 2025 ; Men et al. 2024 ) . Causal-intervention methods likewise localize behavior by patching activations at chosen sites ( Meng et al. 2022 ; Wang et al. 2023 ; Goldowsky-Dill et al. 2023 ; Chan et al. 2022 ; Zhang and Nanda 2024 ) ; the cross-layer attribution methods of Lindsey et al. (2024) , Dunefsky et al. (2024) , and Lindsey et al. (2025) are closest in spirit, but decompose the representation into features spanning layers. We instead decompose the function : whether one layer’s write changes how later layers compute, including effects requiring three or more layers jointly, with the residual identity as the null—the only value under which U T U_{T} vanishes exactly when a participating layer is removed (Section 5.3 contrasts the resulting block-removal rankings with similarity-based ones). Residual networks have been read as ensembles of shallow paths ( Veit et al. 2016 ) or as iterative inference ( Jastrzębski et al. 2018 ) ; the former enumerates subpaths, whereas we isolate what the full path contributes beyond every proper subpath. Formally, our estimand is the Möbius transform, or Harsanyi dividend, of the set function induced by layer ablation ( Harsanyi 1963 ; Grabisch and Roubens 1999 ) , standard for input features and tokens ( Sundararajan et al. 2020 ; Tsai et al. 2023 ; Hao et al. 2021 ) . We differ in that the payoff is a vector-valued residual write, the players are noncommutative maps, and the residual-identity null makes the decomposition exact; connecting to studies of training dynamics ( Nanda et al. 2023 ; Olsson et al. 2022 ; Hoogland et al. 2024 ) , we track this quantity across pretraining, asking not what a model represents but how many layers must act together before a computation exists at all. 3 Cross-Layer Coordination The number of layers the architecture supplies must be distinguished from the depth the trained model actually uses: if each layer edited the residual stream independently of the computations before it, the model would behave less like a deep computation than like a collection of independent refinements applied in sequence. U ^ T \widehat{U}_{T} therefore measures the magnitude of the order- k k connected component relative to the actual write of the final participating layer. This normalization expresses the connected component in units of the local write scale of layer ℓ k \ell_{k} , rather than in absolute residual units. It does not separately normalize the magnitudes of the preceding layers’ updates, whose effects enter through the subset-conditioned inputs F S ​ ( h ) F^{S}(h) . When U ^ T \widehat{U}_{T} is close to 0. Layer ℓ k \ell_{k} ’s update does not require the joint computation of the preceding layers. This covers not only the case where layer ℓ k \ell_{k} writes the same update regardless of what the preceding layers computed, but also the case where each preceding layer does change the update, yet the change reduces to a sum of per-layer contributions. In the latter case layer ℓ k \ell_{k} coordinates with the preceding layers only individually, and such lower-order coordination cancels exactly in the alternating sum of Eq. ( 8 ). Either way, no order- k k coordination exists. When U ^ T \widehat{U}_{T} is close to 1. The order- k k connected component has a magnitude comparable to the actual update written by layer ℓ k \ell_{k} when all preceding participating layers are present. Thus, the joint interaction associated with all layers in T T is large relative to the local write scale of the final participating layer. Importantly, U ^ T \widehat{U}_{T} should not be interpreted as the fraction of layer ℓ k \ell_{k} ’s update attributable to order- k k coordination, because the connected and lower-order components need not be orthogonal. For the same reason, U ^ T \widehat{U}_{T} is not bounded above by 1: U T U_{T} is an alternating combination of actual and counterfactual updates, and its norm can exceed that of the actual write used for normalization. Because the baseline value of U ^ T \widehat{U}_{T} decreases with interaction order, R k R_{k} should be interpreted within each order rather than as an absolute comparison of interaction strength across orders. 4 Experimental Setup Models. We use public checkpoints of Pythia ( Biderman et al. 2023 ) , OLMo ( Groeneveld et al. 2024 ) , and Amber ( Liu et al. 2023 ) . All three families release intermediate pretraining checkpoints, which lets us track how coordination is organized over the course of training within a fixed architecture. Using families that differ in scale, depth, and training data guards against the observations being a property of any single model family. The models and checkpoints are summarized in Table 1 . We restrict to adjacent windows so that the subset forward passes and the full forward pass share the same input state and bypass no intermediate layer, keeping the site of the deletion intervention well defined. During the full forward pass we record the base point h h at the input of ℓ 1 \ell_{1} , run the 2 k 2^{k} subset forward passes separately to compute U T ​ ( h ) U_{T}(h) , subtract it from the residual stream immediately after the output of block ℓ k \ell_{k} , and run the remaining layers unchanged. Because subset composition preserves depth order, the alternating sum of Eq. ( 8 ) resolves exactly into the write of the last participating layer, so the intervention site is determined structurally as ℓ k \ell_{k} rather than by approximation. The deletion thus leaves the model to continue computing from the best subset-explainable reconstruction of its own state. The random control subtracts, at the same site, a Gaussian direction rescaled per token to ∥ U T ∥ \lVert U_{T}\rVert . The two interventions match in norm exactly at the point of action, so any difference in damage is attributable solely to whether the deleted direction is the connected component. items.content: Back to Articles Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run Published November 16, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 116 +110 Célina Hanouti celinah Follow Victor Mustar victor Follow Bertrand Chevrier kramp Follow Lucain Pouget Wauplin Follow Pierric Cistac pierric Follow Eliott Coyac coyotte508 Follow Julien Chaumond julien-c Follow Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request. Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same. Run them with the tools you already use The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent: Setup guides for Claude Code , Codex , OpenCode , Pi and Hermes Agent The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets , compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints . PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference. How open-weight models are used On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July ( OpenRouter, October 2026 ). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens ( rankings ). Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models. The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it. Routing powered by OpenRouter OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic. OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing : instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability. When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%. Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id: zai-org/GLM-5.3 # default: best mix of price, speed and reliability zai-org/GLM-5.3:fastest # highest throughput zai-org/GLM-5.3:cheapest # lowest price zai-org/GLM-5.3:novita # only Novita Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide ). Pricing Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details. Image, video and audio generation Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs . See where your requests go On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request. Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same. Run them with the tools you already use The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent: Setup guides for Claude Code , Codex , OpenCode , Pi and Hermes Agent The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets , compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints . PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference. How open-weight models are used On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July ( OpenRouter, October 2026 ). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens ( rankings ). Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models. The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54).
