items.content: A Methodologically Rigorous Benchmark of Linear Regression, RNN, and LSTM for S&P 500 Forecasting: Identifying Sources of Performance Inflation in Financial Deep Learning Hari Sitaula † † thanks: Assistant Professor Department of Mathematical Sciences hsitaula@mtech.edu Joseph Opitz † † thanks: jopitz@mtech.edu Abstract This study examines one-day-ahead forecasting of the S&P 500 closing level using a 2006–2025 dataset that uses fundamental price data, macroeconomic indicators, and engineered technical features. We benchmark three model families, namely linear regression, vanilla recurrent neural networks (RNN), and long short-term memory networks (LSTM), within a unified preprocessing and chronological evaluation pipeline. A central contribution of this work is a methodological audit into common practices in the deep-learning-for-stock-prediction literature. We identify three sources of result inflation that frequently appear in published methodology: wavelet-denoised evaluation targets, the absence of a naive persistence baseline, and best-of- N N replicate reporting. We then re-evaluate all model families under a corrected protocol that controls for each. Performance is reported using root mean squared error, mean absolute percentage error, and the Pearson correlation coefficient, averaged across N = 30 N=30 independent replicates per configuration. We compare models on accuracy, stability across replicates, and architectural depth sensitivity, using the naive persistence forecast (predicting today’s close as tomorrow’s close) as a primary baseline against which all candidate models must demonstrate improvement. Affiliation: Department of Mathematical Sciences, Montana Technological University, 1300 W Park St, Butte, MT 59701, USA. Keywords: Stock market forecasting, S&P 500, Linear regression, Recurrent neural networks, Long short-term memory, Time series modeling, Financial machine learning, Methodology audit, Naive baseline 1 Introduction The problem of forecasting financial markets has attracted scholarly attention for well over a century. Early theoretical treatments characterized asset prices as a random walk ( Bachelier, 2011 ) , a view later formalized through the efficient-markets hypothesis, which holds that publicly available information is rapidly impounded into prices, leaving little room for systematic short-horizon predictability ( Samuelson, 1965 ; Fama, 1970 ) . Subsequent econometric work acknowledged that while prices may approximate a martingale, their higher-order dynamics (autocorrelation in returns, volatility clustering, and cross-series co-movement) could nonetheless be modeled using ARIMA, VAR, and ARCH/GARCH frameworks ( Hyndman and Athanasopoulos, 2021 ; Engle, 2004b ) . The empirical discovery of persistent anomalies, including momentum and value premia, further established that statistical structure in market data is not entirely arbitraged away ( Jegadeesh and Titman, 1993 ; Fama and French, 1992 ) . As computational resources expanded, the dominant paradigm shifted toward machine learning methods capable of accommodating nonlinearity and high-dimensional feature interactions, and more recently toward deep sequence models, particularly recurrent neural networks and their gated variants, that learn state-dependent temporal representations directly from raw multivariate inputs ( Nabipour et al., 2020 ; Zou et al., 2022 ) . Beyond academic interest, accurate forecasting carries tangible economic consequences: even modest predictive edges translate into improvements in algorithmic execution quality, tighter bid–ask spreads, and stronger market liquidity ( Hendershott et al., 2011 ) , while also underpinning the risk-management frameworks central to global financial stability ( Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, 2019 ) . The practical value of short-horizon forecasting extends across multiple dimensions of institutional finance. At the execution level, one-day-ahead signals improve order timing and inventory control, reducing slippage and reinforcing price discovery ( Hendershott et al., 2011 ) . At the risk-management level, they inform Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall estimates used by trading desks and regulators under frameworks such as the Basel Accords ( Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, 2019 ) . At the portfolio level, even modest directional accuracy in index-level forecasts can compound meaningfully through improved entry and exit timing, provided that transaction costs and market impact are explicitly accounted for ( Fleming et al., 2003 ) . The modeling landscape for financial time-series forecasting has evolved through three broadly sequential generations. Classical statistical models such as ARIMA, VAR, and GARCH remain competitive baselines when return dynamics are approximately linear and stationary, but they impose structural constraints that limit their ability to capture regime-dependent nonlinearities and heteroskedastic volatility. Classical machine learning methods, including regularized linear models, support vector machines, and tree-based ensembles, relax some of these constraints once features are manually engineered from price lags, technical indicators, and macroeconomic variables ( Gu et al., 2020 ) . Deep learning architectures, particularly one-dimensional CNNs, vanilla RNNs, gated recurrent units (GRUs), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, go further by learning hierarchical temporal representations and state-dependent nonlinearities directly from multivariate sequences, often improving short-horizon accuracy under disciplined validation ( Bhandari et al., 2022 ) . In an influential index-level study, Bhandari et al. (2022) construct a fused feature set combining fundamental price data, macroeconomic indicators (VIX, EFFR, UNRATE, UMCSENT, USDX), and technical signals (MACD, ATR, RSI), and report that a single-layer LSTM predicting one-day-ahead S&P 500 closing levels outperforms deeper multi-layer stacks on RMSE, MAPE, and the correlation coefficient R R . A recurring concern in the deep-learning-for-stock-prediction literature is that reported performance gains can be sensitive to evaluation methodology. These indicators are calculated using daily closing prices and intraday ranges, and are included as additional input features for all models. The MACD measures short-term momentum by comparing fast and slow exponential moving averages of the price series. By capturing changes in trend direction and momentum strength, the MACD provides information about market acceleration that may not be evident from raw price levels alone. Momentum-based indicators such as MACD have been documented to contain predictive structure in equity markets, particularly over short horizons ( Jegadeesh and Titman, 1993 ; Nabipour et al., 2020 ) . ATR is a volatility-based indicator that summarizes the magnitude of daily price fluctuations. Unlike simple return variance, ATR reflects intraday price ranges and is sensitive to abrupt volatility spikes, which are common during periods of market stress. Volatility-related features are especially relevant for forecasting models operating across multiple market regimes, as volatility dynamics often change more rapidly than price levels ( Engle, 2004a ) . RSI is a bounded momentum oscillator that measures the relative strength of recent gains versus losses. By normalizing momentum information to a fixed scale, RSI helps identify overbought and oversold conditions and provides nonlinear transformations of price dynamics that can be particularly useful for machine learning models ( Nabipour et al., 2020 ; Zou et al., 2022 ) . Together, these indicators complement the fundamental price variables by encoding trend, momentum, and volatility information in a compact form. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.27970 (cs) [Submitted on 20 Nov 2026] Title: On the Complete Feature Set for ADHD Classification in Children and Adolescents Based on EEG Signals Authors: Javier Sanchis , Álvaro Navarro , Jorge García-Carrasco , Tahar Kechadi , Juan Trujillo View a PDF of the paper titled On the Complete Feature Set for ADHD Classification in Children and Adolescents Based on EEG Signals, by Javier Sanchis and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition that can affect attention, activity and impulse control. Electroencephalography (EEG) records brain activity as children and adolescents perform cognitive tasks. However, comparing features derived from these recordings requires consistent signal preparation, shared analysis windows and documented quality decisions. We curated 669 existing BALLADEER recordings from 156 participants across five task conditions so that researchers can compare seven EEG feature families on the same time intervals for each participant and task. The dataset links continuous signals to precomputed measurements from 115 feature definitions or templates and records the quality decisions made for each recording. Analyses must still account for repeated measurements within participants, residual artefacts and differences between acquisition systems. Technical validation covered signal integrity, numerical checks on feature estimators and completeness of the released files. In every task, the median proportion of recording time retained after preprocessing was 100%. To illustrate reuse, we report saved participant-held-out evaluations comparing XGBoost using all seven families on eight-second windows with a predictor based only on recruitment-group prevalence in the training fold. Recruitment-group discrimination was stronger in Robots than in the three Slackline conditions. These descriptive results from overlapping cohorts do not establish diagnostic validity. The dataset, curation software and aggregate results for the predictive example are publicly available. Comments: 28 pages, 7 figures. items.content: On the Complete Feature Set for ADHD Classification in Children and Adolescents Based on EEG Signals Javier Sanchis a,* , Álvaro Navarro a , Jorge García-Carrasco a , Tahar Kechadi b , Juan Trujillo a a Lucentia Research, Department of Software and Computing Systems, University of Alicante, Carretera San Vicente del Raspeig s/n, Sant Vicent del Raspeig, 03690, Alicante, Spain b School of Computer Science and Informatics, University College Dublin, Belfield, Dublin 4, D04 V1W8, Ireland * Corresponding author: Javier Sanchis, javier.sanchis@ua.es Keywords: EEG, ADHD, Signal preprocessing, Feature extraction, Quality control, Research data Abstract Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition that can affect attention, activity and impulse control. Electroencephalography (EEG) records brain activity as children and adolescents perform cognitive tasks. However, comparing features derived from these recordings requires consistent signal preparation, shared analysis windows and documented quality decisions. We curated 669 existing BALLADEER recordings from 156 participants across five task conditions so that researchers can compare seven EEG feature families on the same time intervals for each participant and task. The dataset links continuous signals to precomputed measurements from 115 feature definitions or templates and records the quality decisions made for each recording. Analyses must still account for repeated measurements within participants, residual artefacts and differences between acquisition systems. Technical validation covered signal integrity, numerical checks on feature estimators and completeness of the released files. In every task, the median proportion of recording time retained after preprocessing was 100%. To illustrate reuse, we report saved participant-held-out evaluations comparing XGBoost using all seven families on eight-second windows with a predictor based only on recruitment-group prevalence in the training fold. Recruitment-group discrimination was stronger in Robots than in the three Slackline conditions. These descriptive results from overlapping cohorts do not establish diagnostic validity. The dataset, curation software and aggregate results for the predictive example are publicly available. 1 Introduction Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterised by persistent inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interferes with everyday functioning. Its heterogeneous presentation motivates research into complementary measurements of the processes underlying these behaviours. Clinical diagnosis requires assessment of developmental history, symptoms and functioning across settings. Electroencephalography (EEG) provides non-invasive measurements of electrical brain activity that can support this research, including investigation of candidate neurophysiological markers during cognitive tasks. These measurements complement the study of ADHD but do not, by themselves, constitute an established diagnostic test [ 1 , 2 ] . A central approach to analysing EEG is to derive features: numerical descriptions of properties such as signal amplitude, oscillatory power, irregularity and relationships between electrodes. These representations make particular signal properties explicit and provide inputs for statistical analysis, feature selection and machine learning. Recent EEG–ADHD literature includes spectral, entropy and connectivity measures, reflecting interest in complementary descriptions of brain activity [ 3 ] . Engineered features also complement approaches that learn representations directly from signals. Retaining continuous EEG alongside precomputed features therefore enables researchers to investigate both approaches and examine how representation choices affect downstream findings. Public datasets provide an essential foundation for such work. Existing resources include paediatric attention-task recordings and broader transdiagnostic collections such as the Healthy Brain Network [ 4 , 5 ] . The BALLADEER dataset extends this landscape with EEG recorded during cognitive activities alongside behavioural, cognitive and other physiological measurements. Its EEG recordings cover CogniFit, Attention Robots and selected levels of Attention Slackline, providing opportunities to investigate representations across different recording contexts [ 6 ] . However, access to recordings does not itself provide the aligned signals, feature definitions and quality information needed to compare representations on matched data. In BALLADEER, reuse requires accounting for acquisition-system differences, recording discontinuities and channel problems before defining analysis windows and computing features. When studies intended to compare representations use different preparation procedures or recording intervals, their findings can also reflect these choices. Automated EEG pipelines already demonstrate the value of documented preprocessing and feature extraction [ 7 ] . For these task recordings, the remaining need is a reusable collection that links the resulting measurements to their source intervals, curation decisions and calculation states. To address these reuse barriers, we prepared a secondary curated resource containing 669 eligible recordings from 156 children and adolescents across five task conditions: CogniFit, Robots and selected levels of Slackline. The resource retains continuous EEG alongside complementary feature tables and source-linked quality records. It uses established processing methods without recruiting a new cohort or treating the different acquisition systems as equivalent. Its contribution is the additional curation information, aligned measurements and documented computational definitions made available for reuse. The resource makes four contributions: • Auditable signal derivatives. Label-blind eligibility decisions, expert quality assessments and processing records accompany curated continuous EEG, allowing researchers to inspect how recordings were selected and transformed. • Aligned multi-family representations. Seven feature families encompass 115 definitions or templates computed on shared analysis intervals. Explicit calculation states distinguish unavailable or undefined measurements, while catalogues document their indexed expansion across channels and other positions. • Documented validation and reproduction resources. Numerical reference checks, structural integrity checks, configurations and preparation software support inspection and reproduction of the released derivatives. • A participant-held-out baseline for reuse. Across four overlapping task cohorts, saved evaluations compare XGBoost using all seven feature families on eight-second windows with a predictor that assigns every held-out participant the proportion of ADHD recruits in the training fold. These retrospective results illustrate recruitment-group discrimination, which was weaker in Slackline than in Robots; they do not establish diagnostic validity. The resource supports representation comparisons, feature-selection research and alternative signal analyses, provided that reuse accounts for participant dependence, residual artefacts and task-device differences. 2 Materials and Methods The curation workflow combines source auditing, conservative preprocessing selected from technical Quality Control (QC) evidence, and aligned feature extraction (Figure 1 ). Clinical and demographic labels did not determine eligibility, preprocessing or feature values. The release links the processed signals and features to their QC and processing records. Figure 1: EEG curation workflow, from source inventory to aligned feature extraction. 2.1 Source data and cohort 2.1.1 Source dataset, participants and ethics This resource derives from five EEG tasks in the publicly available BALLADEER dataset [ 6 , 8 ] . Pseudonymous identifiers support linkage to compatible source records. The original recordings and non-EEG modalities remain in the source dataset. The source demographic file contains 158 participant records. This resource includes 669 eligible task recordings from 156 of those participants. In the full source cohort, participants were aged 6-18 years, with 96 coded as male and 62 as female. Participants were asked to discontinue ADHD medication for at least 24 hours before collection [ 6 ] . The field group distinguishes 62 participants recruited with a formal pre-existing ADHD diagnosis from 96 recruited as comparisons. The separate field diagnosed records the clinical team’s assessment-derived status as yes , no , or undetermined . It is not equivalent to pre-existing diagnosis. All ADHD recruits have status yes , whereas the comparison group contains all three outcomes and should not be treated as clinically confirmed healthy controls. Table 1 cross-classifies these fields, which were excluded from processing decisions. Table 1: Recruitment and assessment-derived label composition. Group Group total Diagnosed yes no undetermined ADHD recruitment 62 62 0 0 Control recruitment 96 26 50 20 The original study received approval from the University of Alicante Ethics Committee (UA-2023-05-17_1) and the ISABIAL Ethics Committee (PI2022-139). Participants or their legal guardians, as applicable, provided written consent for participation, collection, and anonymised public sharing [ 6 ] . No new recruitment or acquisition was undertaken. 2.1.2 Experimental tasks and EEG acquisition The five task conditions comprised CogniFit, Robots (Attention Robots), and Slackline L1, L6 and L11, where L denotes the Attention Slackline level. CogniFit involved adaptive exercises in perception, attention, coordination, and problem solving. Robots required participants to select robots matching target criteria in a 14 × 47 14\times 47 grid, with 20 seconds per row. Slackline comprised five-minute levels 1, 6, and 11, in which participants pressed a button in response to on-screen flag patterns to control an avatar’s progress. These levels required matching one target, either of two targets, or a two-target sequence, respectively [ 9 , 6 ] . EEG spanned task onset to completion, excluding tutorial or instruction intervals. No dedicated resting-state condition was collected. Task identifiers and acquisition characteristics are summarised in Table 2 . Prior behavioural work described and validated Slackline [ 9 ] . A separate study of Robots reported preliminary behavioural convergent validity against D2-R [ 10 ] . That study’s behavioural sample and outcomes do not establish EEG or diagnostic validity for the present resource. Table 2: Source EEG tasks and acquisition characteristics. Source task ID Brief protocol Acquisition CogniFit BAL01 Adaptive computerized cognitive exercises EPOC X/Plus, 128 or 256 Hz Robots BAL02 Visual search for robots matching target criteria EPOC X/Plus, 128 or 256 Hz Slackline L1 BAL03 Button response to one on-screen flag target CGX Quick-32r, 500 Hz Slackline L6 BAL04 Button response to either of two on-screen flag targets CGX Quick-32r, 500 Hz Slackline L11 BAL05 Button response to an on-screen two-flag sequence CGX Quick-32r, 500 Hz CogniFit and Robots used 14-channel Emotiv EPOC X or EPOC Plus at 128 Hz, except seven EPOC Plus recordings in the valid 256-Hz mode. The Slackline tasks used CGX Quick-32r at 500 Hz, contributing 29 scalp EEG channels. Operators checked vendor sensor-contact indicators before each session [ 6 ] . Adapters converted amplitudes to volts and assigned standard 10-20 template coordinates, not participant-specific digitisations. Emotiv streams included vendor Sinc and notch conditioning, whereas CGX retained minimal hardware conditioning. No common offline processing or undocumented acquisition reference was assumed at ingestion. Task, device, montage, and duration differences preclude treating the tasks as interchangeable conditions. 2.1.3 Source data audit and recording eligibility The audit enumerated 158 × 5 = 790 158\times 5=790 participant-task combinations, checked agreement between metadata and directories, located EEG CSV files, and required readable samples and valid timestamps. Missing tasks were recorded as unavailable. Relative paths and input checksums preserve source identity. For N N samples with first and last valid timestamps t 1 , t N t_{1},t_{N} , duration was T = t N − t 1 T=t_{N}-t_{1} and effective sampling frequency was f eff = ( N − 1 ) / T f_{\mathrm{eff}}=(N-1)/T . Within each task, duration outside [ P 10 − 1.5 ​ ( P 90 − P 10 ) , P 90 + 1.5 ​ ( P 90 − P 10 ) ] [P_{10}-1.5(P_{90}-P_{10}),\,P_{90}+1.5(P_{90}-P_{10})] was flagged. Sampling frequency failed independently when | f eff − f expected | / f expected > 0.20 |f_{\mathrm{eff}}-f_{\mathrm{expected}}|/f_{\mathrm{expected}}>0.20 , using the Emotiv header value or 500 Hz for CGX. Eligibility outcomes are reported in Section 4.1 . Absence or failure in one task did not exclude a participant’s other recordings. Audit tables retain each measurement and decision reason. 2.2 Quality characterisation and preprocessing Measurements at window, channel, and recording scales informed label-blind selection and a gap-aware preprocessing sequence. 2.2.1 Raw EEG quality characterisation Raw QC combined 4s temporal, 8s spectral, and full-recording measurements before offline processing. This multiscale approach drew on established EEG quality frameworks [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] and reporting recommendations [ 16 ] . Measurements were compared within task-acquisition strata for EPOC X, EPOC Plus, and CGX, accounting for device-dependent spectra [ 17 ] . They indicate technical integrity or possible contamination, not biological normality [ 18 ] . Table 3 lists the retained measurements. Table 3: Raw EEG QC measurements retained at each analysis scale. Analysis scale QC measurements 4s temporal windows (50% overlap) Finite-sample, Not a Number, and infinity fractions, Standard Deviation, Median Absolute Deviation, median-centred Root Mean Square, peak-to-peak amplitude, maximum absolute derivative, line length, flat-sample and repeated-value fractions, longest flat run, skewness, Fisher excess kurtosis, median-centred zero-crossing rate, median pairwise Spearman channel correlation, and median Global Field Power. 8s spectral windows (50% overlap) Absolute and relative delta, theta, alpha, beta, and high-beta power, slow-drift ratio, common and extended high-frequency ratios, 50-Hz line-noise ratio and supported harmonics, spectral entropy, Theil-Sen spectral slope, 95% spectral edge frequency, median pairwise spectral correlation, and median absolute spectral deviation. Full recording Recorded and usable duration, expected and observed sampling frequency, signed sampling-frequency error, interval jitter, duplicate and backward timestamps, invalid-row count, gap count and duration, continuous-block count, channel inventory, full-recording median channel and nearest-neighbour correlations, and persistent spectral deviation. Both window scales used 50% overlap, excluded incomplete windows, and never crossed gaps. Values were summarised within recordings before calibration, so overlapping windows were not treated as independent observations. The scales balance temporal localisation and spectral support rather than represent empirically established optima [ 19 , 20 ] . Temporal metrics included Standard Deviation (SD), Median Absolute Deviation (MAD), and median-centred Root Mean Square (RMS). Flat and repeated-value fractions used a 10 − 9 10^{-9} V change threshold. Median-centred zero crossings used a ± 1 ​ μ \pm 1\,\mu V dead-band. No temporal metric alone established exclusion. Spectral QC used Welch Power Spectral Density (PSD) estimates with 4s Hamming segments, 50% overlap, constant detrending, mean averaging, and density scaling. Each 8s window supplied three segments and a 0.25-Hz grid. Absolute and relative powers in 1–4, 4–8, 8–13, 13–30, and 30–40 Hz were descriptive and could not independently trigger rejection. Technical ratios covered 0.5–1, 30–40, and, where supported, 40–100 Hz. The line-noise ratio compared 50 ± 1 50\pm 1 Hz power with adjacent 2-Hz bands. Recording-scale checks assessed clocks, channel inventory, continuity, and persistent channel behaviour. A timestamp gap exceeded 1.5 / f expected 1.5/f_{\mathrm{expected}} , with missing duration G = ∑ i max ⁡ ( 0 , Δ ​ t i − f expected − 1 ) G=\sum_{i}\max(0,\Delta t_{i}-f_{\mathrm{expected}}^{-1}) . EPOC observed sampling frequency was the inverse median positive timestamp interval. For CGX, timestamp span described transport rate, while the sample counter defined discontinuities and the analysis clock. Gap count, duration, and block count were retained separately. Every metric included units, parameters, source segments, and a state of computed, not computable, not applicable, or invalid input. 2.2.2 QC interpretation and preprocessing selection Metrics had prespecified roles as integrity failures, robust warnings, descriptive evidence, or unavailable evidence. Nonfinite input, invalid rows, duplicate or backward timestamps, and channel-inventory violations used absolute rules. Warning thresholds used one profile per recording-task rather than pooled overlapping windows. The calibration subset comprised 60% of each task-acquisition stratum, capped at 80 participants. For calibration median m m , s = 1.4826 ​ MAD s=1.4826\,\mathrm{MAD} , and quantile Q Q , the direction-specific limits were U = max ⁡ { Q 0.99 , m + 6 ​ s } , L = min ⁡ { Q 0.01 , m − 6 ​ s } . U=\max\{Q_{0.99},m+6s\},\qquad L=\min\{Q_{0.01},m-6s\}. The MAD scaling constant provides Gaussian consistency without requiring normally distributed metrics [ 21 , 22 ] . These conservative limits flagged technical extremes. Biology-sensitive metrics, including band power and spectral edge, could not independently trigger rejection or preprocessing. Clinical, demographic, and downstream outcome variables were unavailable during calibration. We assessed persistence using the proportion of affected windows and their combined non-overlapping duration. A recording warning required at least 5% affected channel-window evidence. Interpolation recommendations required at least three warning metrics spanning three independent mechanisms [ 12 , 13 ] . Automatic states were pass , pass with warnings , or review . Recommendations alone did not alter samples. Experts checked the signal quality of 103 selected recording-task pairs without access to clinical labels, examining signal traces, PSD, timing integrity, spatial patterns, and 4s/8s quality measurements. Their assessments helped determine which recordings to exclude and which channels to interpolate, while the calibrated automatic thresholds remained unchanged. The assessments, decisions, and reasons are documented in the released QC records. Unresolved review states were retained with warnings under the conservative policy. Final exclusion counts are reported in Section 4.2 . 2.2.3 Preprocessing and derivative generation The same preprocessing operations were applied to EPOC and CGX recordings, with acquisition-specific QC warning thresholds. Continuous blocks were processed independently using a fourth-order zero-phase Butterworth second-order-section filter at 0.5–40 Hz [ 23 ] . Polyphase anti-alias resampling converted 256-Hz and 500-Hz input to 128 Hz. Native 128-Hz recordings retained their sampling rate. Blocks no longer than 1 s could be omitted only when cumulative omission did not exceed 0.1% of recording duration. Approved channels were interpolated using inverse-distance weighting from the four nearest valid template electrodes, capped at 10% of the montage. Average reference followed interpolation. Every omission and channel action was logged. Each eligible recording yielded one MNE-FIF signal file with channel order, montage information, boundary annotations, and records linking it to the source and applied processing. Postprocessing QC repeated compatible raw measurements to assess retained duration, channel actions, continuity, and expected temporal, spectral, and connectivity changes. items.raw_text: On the Complete Feature Set for ADHD Classification in Children and Adolescents Based on EEG Signals Javier Sanchis a,* , Álvaro Navarro a , Jorge García-Carrasco a , Tahar Kechadi b , Juan Trujillo a a Lucentia Research, Department of Software and Computing Systems, University of Alicante, Carretera San Vicente del Raspeig s/n, Sant Vicent del Raspeig, 03690, Alicante, Spain b School of Computer Science and Informatics, University College Dublin, Belfield, Dublin 4, D04 V1W8, Ireland * Corresponding author: Javier Sanchis, javier.sanchis@ua.es Keywords: EEG, ADHD, Signal preprocessing, Feature extraction, Quality control, Research data Abstract Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition that can affect attention, activity and impulse control. Electroencephalography (EEG) records brain activity as children and adolescents perform cognitive tasks. However, comparing features derived from these recordings requires consistent signal preparation, shared analysis windows and documented quality decisions. We curated 669 existing BALLADEER recordings from 156 participants across five task conditions so that researchers can compare seven EEG feature families on the same time intervals for each participant and task. The dataset links continuous signals to precomputed measurements from 115 feature definitions or templates and records the quality decisions made for each recording. Analyses must still account for repeated measurements within participants, residual artefacts and differences between acquisition systems. Technical validation covered signal integrity, numerical checks on feature estimators and completeness of the released files. In every task, the median proportion of recording time retained after preprocessing was 100%. To illustrate reuse, we report saved participant-held-out evaluations comparing XGBoost using all seven families on eight-second windows with a predictor based only on recruitment-group prevalence in the training fold. Recruitment-group discrimination was stronger in Robots than in the three Slackline conditions. These descriptive results from overlapping cohorts do not establish diagnostic validity. The dataset, curation software and aggregate results for the predictive example are publicly available. 1 Introduction Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterised by persistent inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interferes with everyday functioning. Its heterogeneous presentation motivates research into complementary measurements of the processes underlying these behaviours. Clinical diagnosis requires assessment of developmental history, symptoms and functioning across settings. Electroencephalography (EEG) provides non-invasive measurements of electrical brain activity that can support this research, including investigation of candidate neurophysiological markers during cognitive tasks. These measurements complement the study of ADHD but do not, by themselves, constitute an established diagnostic test [ 1 , 2 ] . A central approach to analysing EEG is to derive features: numerical descriptions of properties such as signal amplitude, oscillatory power, irregularity and relationships between electrodes. These representations make particular signal properties explicit and provide inputs for statistical analysis, feature selection and machine learning. Recent EEG–ADHD literature includes spectral, entropy and connectivity measures, reflecting interest in complementary descriptions of brain activity [ 3 ] . Engineered features also complement approaches that learn representations directly from signals. Retaining continuous EEG alongside precomputed features therefore enables researchers to investigate both approaches and examine how representation choices affect downstream findings. Public datasets provide an essential foundation for such work. Existing resources include paediatric attention-task recordings and broader transdiagnostic collections such as the Healthy Brain Network [ 4 , 5 ] . The BALLADEER dataset extends this landscape with EEG recorded during cognitive activities alongside behavioural, cognitive and other physiological measurements. Its EEG recordings cover CogniFit, Attention Robots and selected levels of Attention Slackline, providing opportunities to investigate representations across different recording contexts [ 6 ] . However, access to recordings does not itself provide the aligned signals, feature definitions and quality information needed to compare representations on matched data. In BALLADEER, reuse requires accounting for acquisition-system differences, recording discontinuities and channel problems before defining analysis windows and computing features. When studies intended to compare representations use different preparation procedures or recording intervals, their findings can also reflect these choices. Automated EEG pipelines already demonstrate the value of documented preprocessing and feature extraction [ 7 ] . For these task recordings, the remaining need is a reusable collection that links the resulting measurements to their source intervals, curation decisions and calculation states. To address these reuse barriers, we prepared a secondary curated resource containing 669 eligible recordings from 156 children and adolescents across five task conditions: CogniFit, Robots and selected levels of Slackline. The resource retains continuous EEG alongside complementary feature tables and source-linked quality records. It uses established processing methods without recruiting a new cohort or treating the different acquisition systems as equivalent. Its contribution is the additional curation information, aligned measurements and documented computational definitions made available for reuse. The resource makes four contributions: • Auditable signal derivatives. Label-blind eligibility decisions, expert quality assessments and processing records accompany curated continuous EEG, allowing researchers to inspect how recordings were selected and transformed. • Aligned multi-family representations. Seven feature families encompass 115 definitions or templates computed on shared analysis intervals. Explicit calculation states distinguish unavailable or undefined measurements, while catalogues document their indexed expansion across channels and other positions. • Documented validation and reproduction resources. Numerical reference checks, structural integrity checks, configurations and preparation software support inspection and reproduction of the released derivatives. • A participant-held-out baseline for reuse. Across four overlapping task cohorts, saved evaluations compare XGBoost using all seven feature families on eight-second windows with a predictor that assigns every held-out participant the proportion of ADHD recruits in the training fold. These retrospective results illustrate recruitment-group discrimination, which was weaker in Slackline than in Robots; they do not establish diagnostic validity. The resource supports representation comparisons, feature-selection research and alternative signal analyses, provided that reuse accounts for participant dependence, residual artefacts and task-device differences. 2 Materials and Methods The curation workflow combines source auditing, conservative preprocessing selected from technical Quality Control (QC) evidence, and aligned feature extraction (Figure 1 ). Clinical and demographic labels did not determine eligibility, preprocessing or feature values. The release links the processed signals and features to their QC and processing records. Figure 1: EEG curation workflow, from source inventory to aligned feature extraction. 2.1 Source data and cohort 2.1.1 Source dataset, participants and ethics This resource derives from five EEG tasks in the publicly available BALLADEER dataset [ 6 , 8 ] . Pseudonymous identifiers support linkage to compatible source records. The original recordings and non-EEG modalities remain in the source dataset. The source demographic file contains 158 participant records. This resource includes 669 eligible task recordings from 156 of those participants. In the full source cohort, participants were aged 6-18 years, with 96 coded as male and 62 as female. Participants were asked to discontinue ADHD medication for at least 24 hours before collection [ 6 ] . The field group distinguishes 62 participants recruited with a formal pre-existing ADHD diagnosis from 96 recruited as comparisons. The separate field diagnosed records the clinical team’s assessment-derived status as yes , no , or undetermined . It is not equivalent to pre-existing diagnosis. All ADHD recruits have status yes , whereas the comparison group contains all three outcomes and should not be treated as clinically confirmed healthy controls. Table 1 cross-classifies these fields, which were excluded from processing decisions. Table 1: Recruitment and assessment-derived label composition. Group Group total Diagnosed yes no undetermined ADHD recruitment 62 62 0 0 Control recruitment 96 26 50 20 The original study received approval from the University of Alicante Ethics Committee (UA-2023-05-17_1) and the ISABIAL Ethics Committee (PI2022-139). Participants or their legal guardians, as applicable, provided written consent for participation, collection, and anonymised public sharing [ 6 ] . No new recruitment or acquisition was undertaken. 2.1.2 Experimental tasks and EEG acquisition The five task conditions comprised CogniFit, Robots (Attention Robots), and Slackline L1, L6 and L11, where L denotes the Attention Slackline level. CogniFit involved adaptive exercises in perception, attention, coordination, and problem solving. Robots required participants to select robots matching target criteria in a 14 × 47 14\times 47 grid, with 20 seconds per row. Slackline comprised five-minute levels 1, 6, and 11, in which participants pressed a button in response to on-screen flag patterns to control an avatar’s progress. These levels required matching one target, either of two targets, or a two-target sequence, respectively [ 9 , 6 ] . EEG spanned task onset to completion, excluding tutorial or instruction intervals. No dedicated resting-state condition was collected. Task identifiers and acquisition characteristics are summarised in Table 2 . Prior behavioural work described and validated Slackline [ 9 ] . This multiscale approach drew on established EEG quality frameworks [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] and reporting recommendations [ 16 ] . Measurements were compared within task-acquisition strata for EPOC X, EPOC Plus, and CGX, accounting for device-dependent spectra [ 17 ] . They indicate technical integrity or possible contamination, not biological normality [ 18 ] . Table 3 lists the retained measurements. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.27959 (cs) [Submitted on 20 Nov 2026] Title: Ranking-Preserving Coreset Selection for Efficient Evolutionary Hyperparameter Optimization Authors: Mamoona Tasadduq , Maryam Bashir View a PDF of the paper titled Ranking-Preserving Coreset Selection for Efficient Evolutionary Hyperparameter Optimization, by Mamoona Tasadduq and Maryam Bashir View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) is essential for high predictive performance, but its computational cost becomes prohibitive when candidate configurations require repeated training on large datasets. This paper proposes a ranking-preserving coreset (RPC) selection framework for accelerating evolutionary HPO. The method constructs a compact coreset that preserves the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations observed on the full training data. Coreset selection is formulated as an evolutionary optimization problem that maximizes Spearman rank correlation between full-data and subset-based configuration rankings while penalizing subset size. The selected coreset is then used for HPO with three evolutionary algorithms: Genetic Algorithm (GA), Cross-generational elitist Selection, Heterogeneous Recombination and Cataclysmic Mutation (CHC), and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). Experiments on seven tabular, two text, and two image benchmark datasets show that RPC substantially reduces HPO time while maintaining test accuracy comparable to full-dataset HPO across decision tree, text classification, and image classification tasks. Across datasets and optimizers, HPO-stage speedups range from approximately 1.14x to 8.80x, while the one-time coreset construction cost is accounted for separately through end-to-end runtime and break-even analysis. On 20 held-out configurations excluded from coreset construction, RPC achieves higher ranking correlation than same-size random sampling on 8 of 11 datasets (dataset-level Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.014). These results show that ranking preservation extends beyond the configurations used during selection. The one-time construction cost can be amortized when the coreset is reused across HPO runs. items.raw_text: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.27959 (cs) [Submitted on 20 Nov 2026] Title: Ranking-Preserving Coreset Selection for Efficient Evolutionary Hyperparameter Optimization Authors: Mamoona Tasadduq , Maryam Bashir View a PDF of the paper titled Ranking-Preserving Coreset Selection for Efficient Evolutionary Hyperparameter Optimization, by Mamoona Tasadduq and Maryam Bashir View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) is essential for high predictive performance, but its computational cost becomes prohibitive when candidate configurations require repeated training on large datasets. This paper proposes a ranking-preserving coreset (RPC) selection framework for accelerating evolutionary HPO. The method constructs a compact coreset that preserves the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations observed on the full training data. Coreset selection is formulated as an evolutionary optimization problem that maximizes Spearman rank correlation between full-data and subset-based configuration rankings while penalizing subset size. The selected coreset is then used for HPO with three evolutionary algorithms: Genetic Algorithm (GA), Cross-generational elitist Selection, Heterogeneous Recombination and Cataclysmic Mutation (CHC), and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). Experiments on seven tabular, two text, and two image benchmark datasets show that RPC substantially reduces HPO time while maintaining test accuracy comparable to full-dataset HPO across decision tree, text classification, and image classification tasks. Across datasets and optimizers, HPO-stage speedups range from approximately 1.14x to 8.80x, while the one-time coreset construction cost is accounted for separately through end-to-end runtime and break-even analysis. On 20 held-out configurations excluded from coreset construction, RPC achieves higher ranking correlation than same-size random sampling on 8 of 11 datasets (dataset-level Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.014). These results show that ranking preservation extends beyond the configurations used during selection. The one-time construction cost can be amortized when the coreset is reused across HPO runs. Foster , José Jiménez-Luna , Tim Hempel , Sarah Lewis , Yu Xie , Lixin Sun , Iryna Zaporozhets , J. Thorben Frank , Yaoyi Chen , Michael Plainer , Ludwig Winkler , Pedro B. P. S. Reis , Sven H. Giese , Roberto Sordillo , Victor García Satorras , Eray Inanc , Kacper Kapuśniak , Soojung Yang , Rishwanth Raghu , Rachel Kim , Gabriel Dernbach , Deniz Gunceler , Hannes Schulz , Bonnie Kruft , Marwin Segler , Christopher M. Bishop , Cecilia Clementi , Ryota Tomioka , Frank Noé View a PDF of the paper titled BioEmu2: Scalable Emulation of Biomolecular Dynamics, by Michael Gastegger and 29 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Despite major advances in structure prediction, modelling the motions and interactions that drive biomolecular function at scale remains a central challenge. We introduce BioEmu2, a generative model for atomically resolved biomolecular structures combining static structure prediction, equilibrium sampling and time evolution, that samples orders of magnitude faster than molecular dynamics (MD). Trained on experimental and synthetic structures and extensive MD data, it supports multi-component systems containing proteins, nucleic acids, modified residues, ligands and ions. Structure-prediction accuracy is comparable to top open-weight biomolecular folding models, and a context parallel mode enables prediction of megadalton complexes. Equilibrium distributions approximate MD references with free-energy errors near 1 kcal/mol across tested proteins and complexes. Time propagation predicts long-timescale dynamical trajectories and kinetics of binding and conformational changes. Generated structures can be controlled by conditioning on residue contacts or steering with user-defined bias potentials. Enhanced sampling enables free energy calculation involving rare states. BioEmu2 makes the study of biomolecular ensembles and dynamics scalable. Structure-prediction accuracy is comparable to top open-weight biomolecular folding models, and a context parallel mode enables prediction of megadalton complexes. Equilibrium distributions approximate MD references with free-energy errors near 1 kcal/mol across tested proteins and complexes. Time propagation predicts long-timescale dynamical trajectories and kinetics of binding and conformational changes. Generated structures can be controlled by conditioning on residue contacts or steering with user-defined bias potentials. Enhanced sampling enables free energy calculation involving rare states. BioEmu2 makes the study of biomolecular ensembles and dynamics scalable. 1 Introduction Proteins, DNA and RNA form the basic building blocks of life, performing functions from oxygen transport and muscle contraction to storing and processing genetic information. Their activities combine three recurring processes: (i) conformational changes, which alter a molecule’s three-dimensional arrangement; (ii) binding and dissociation, which assemble complexes and capture or release ligands; and (iii) chemical reactions, which transform substrates or act as molecular switches. These processes are often coupled. In haemoglobin for example, oxygen binding shifts the conformational equilibrium from the low-affinity tense (T) state toward the high-affinity relaxed (R) state. This coupling supports cooperative oxygen loading in the lungs and unloading at the lower oxygen partial pressures in tissues [ 1 ] . In adenylate kinase, the catalytic cycle connects nucleotide binding, domain closure, phosphoryl transfer and reopening for product release [ 2 ] . These molecular activities form interconnected pathways that underpin cellular function. A scalable means of understanding molecular function and its disruption in disease could transform drug-target selection, clarify mechanisms of action, and improve predictions of drug efficacy and safety. Next-generation sequencing has made molecular sequences broadly accessible [ 3 ] , while AlphaFold, RoseTTAFold and their all-atom extensions have transformed the prediction of molecular structures and complexes [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] . A predicted structure alone, however, does not specify which conformations are populated, how rapidly they interconvert, or how ligand binding changes these properties. Understanding function therefore requires information about structural ensembles and their dynamics. Biophysical experiments can reveal many aspects of biomolecular function, but usually suffer from either low throughput or low resolution. E.g., cryo-electron microscopy can resolve different conformational states, and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy measures structural fluctuations and exchange processes [ 8 , 9 ] , but both are expensive and require lengthy sample preparation, data collection and data analysis. A broad range of biophysical techniques probe biomolecular shape, dynamics and interactions, including fluorescence and infrared spectroscopy, small-angle X-ray scattering, and hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] . Cell-free expression, miniaturization and cDNA display expand the scale of functional characterization, enabling high-throughput measurements of biochemical activity and protein stability [ 14 , 15 ] . Even when scaled up, these approaches measure low-dimensional observables rather than directly resolving the full atomistic conformational ensemble. Atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) describes the detailed time-resolved evolution of biomolecular structure subject to a chosen force field. Its predictive power is limited by the accuracy of the interaction potential, but especially by the computational cost of adequate sampling. Folding, conformational rearrangements and association can involve rare barrier crossings, requiring extensive simulation timescales, as illustrated by simulations of protein folding and protein–protein association [ 16 , 17 ] . Specialized hardware and enhanced sampling algorithms extend the accessible timescales, but the computational burden of exploring complex conformational landscapes still remains high [ 16 , 17 , 18 ] . Machine-learned coarse-grained models reduce this burden by learning effective interactions for fewer degrees of freedom [ 19 , 20 ] . Recent transferable models reproduce structural and thermodynamic properties of atomistic simulations while achieving orders-of-magnitude computational savings on benchmark proteins [ 20 ] . Yet extending this accuracy across small molecules, recovering atomistic detail and calibrating kinetics remain challenging. Generative models learn to directly sample a target distribution rather than resolving every intervening simulation step. Boltzmann generators sample distributions defined by known energy functions [ 21 ] but have limited capability to scale to large systems. DiG, AlphaFlow and BioEmu learn molecular ensembles from data [ 22 , 23 , 24 ] , but are coarse-grained single-protein models. Timewarp, MDGen and implicit transfer operators extend this approach to time-separated configurations or trajectory segments [ 25 , 26 , 27 ] , but neither of these are biomolecular foundation models that can generalize over a wide range of complex structures. Here we introduce BioEmu2, which unifies three modes in one atomistic framework: (1) structure prediction, with accuracy comparable to current open-weight biomolecular folding models [ 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 ] on FoldBench and Runs N’ Poses [ 32 , 33 ] . (2) approximate room-temperature equilibrium sampling reproducing free energy surfaces of extensive MD simulations within 1 kcal/mol free energy error and covering the major minima; (3) time propagation, which allows structures to be propagated an arbitrary time lag τ \tau in the future, to emulate long-timescale MD trajectories and predict kinetics of conformational changes and binding. BioEmu2 supports multicomponent systems containing proteins, DNA, RNA, modified residues, ligands and ions at heavy-atom resolution. Context parallelism enables inference on systems with over 5000 residues. Contact conditioning and inference-time steering provide control over structure generation. Enhanced sampling improves coverage of rare states, and valid reweighting can recover statistics of the learned base ensemble. Several capabilities remain experimental, particularly slow kinetics, and require larger high-quality experimental datasets and further validation. By accelerating many MD-style sampling tasks by orders of magnitude, BioEmu2 enables rapid iteration toward scalable emulation of biomolecular dynamics and function. 2 BioEmu2 Model BioEmu2 is a generative model that can predict biomolecular structures, ensembles and dynamics with atomistic resolution. In contrast to the first version of BioEmu [ 24 ] , BioEmu2 can model molecular systems consisting of any number of proteins, RNA/DNA, post-translational modifications, lipids, small molecules and ions (Fig. 1 ). We then analyse the performance of BioEmu2 for equilibrium sampling before turning to its modelling of biomolecular kinetics. Finally, we highlight how steering and enhanced sampling techniques offer inference-time control over the obtained ensembles and the quality of generated structures. 3.1 Structure Prediction FoldBench and Runs N’ Poses. We first assess BioEmu2’s ability to predict accurate individual biomolecular structures. In structure prediction mode, the model targets structures characteristic of experimental structure data, such as X-ray crystallography and cryo-EM, rather than an equilibrium ensemble. Using this setting, we compare BioEmu2 to a range of co-folding baseline models on the popular FoldBench benchmark suite [ 32 ] and the Runs N’ Poses benchmark [ 33 ] for protein–ligand bound structure prediction. We selected models for comparison that have a suitable commercial license (excludes AlphaFold3 [ 5 ] ) and a comparable training data cut-off (excludes Boltz-2 [ 39 ] ), resulting in the following baseline methods: Boltz-1 [ 28 ] , ESMFold2 [ 31 ] , OpenFold3 [ 40 ] , Protenix v1 and v2 [ 29 ] and OpenDDE [ 30 ] . We do not use confidence heads when aggregating over multiple samples. The full details of our versions of the two benchmarks are described in Sec. 4.8 . Across both benchmarks, BioEmu2 achieves accuracy competitive with the evaluated co-folding baselines, establishing structure prediction as a core capability of our model (Fig. 2 a,b). Specifically, in the FoldBench results we see that BioEmu2 achieves competitive lDDT [ 41 ] scores for protein and nucleic acid monomers, and attains strong DockQ-based [ 42 ] success rates for chain-to-chain binding. The higher score for protein–protein binding is likely driven by the training data composition, which emphasized protein–protein interaction. The protein–ligand evaluation from Runs N’ Poses also highlights the ability of BioEmu2 to model ligand placement alongside the surrounding protein structure [ 33 ] at a performance level comparable to other strong models. In the comparison presented in Section 3.4 , physicality-steered sampling largely preserves structural prediction accuracy, with modest gains in some categories (Fig. 6 b). Scaling inference to large complexes. BioEmu2’s structural prediction capability extends to larger molecular assemblies. To make larger biomolecular systems accessible at inference time, BioEmu2 implements context parallelism (CP) to distribute pair representations across multiple GPUs [ 43 ] . Benchmarks on NVIDIA B200 GPUs demonstrate scaling from a single GPU to 4 GPUs ( 2 × 2 2\times 2 ) and 16 GPUs ( 4 × 4 4\times 4 ) configurations, supporting systems of up to approximately 16,000 residues. Figure 2 c shows that our CP code substantially extends the maximum accessible system size with manageable communication overhead. At this size, the physicality of the prediction becomes more of a bottleneck than computational feasibility. BioEmu2 preserves both local structural accuracy and overall assembly organization for a wide range of large protein complexes containing thousands of residues. Examples include four multimeric complexes in the test set: 9ISQ (3,508 residues), 8DOL (3,558 residues), 9Q3J (4,040 residues) and 8WW8 (5,832 residues), achieving backbone lDDT scores of 0.81, 0.87, 0.94, and 0.80, global RMSDs of 5.5Å, 5.7 Å, 2.0Å and 6.6 Å respectively (Fig. 2 d). The probability to get successful structure prediction out of the box tends to decrease for increasingly large complexes—both because the structure prediction problem is harder, and because it is often not well-defined as large complexes tend to be assembled in the cell rather than forming in solution. In this case, providing a few additional hints such as residue–residue contacts obtained from experimental knowledge can be sufficient to substantially improve BioEmu2’s predictions. As an example, for the 4,020-residue complex 8WY8, specifying just a single inter-chain contact dramatically improves prediction accuracy, reducing RMSD from 71.2 Å to 5.0 Å and increasing DockQ from 0.10 to 0.46 (Fig. 2 e). 3.2 Equilibrium Sampling In equilibrium mode, BioEmu2 generates independent draws from a learned structural distribution for the specified system. Sampling modes and functional dynamics. BioEmu2 allows to choose between standard structure prediction and equilibrium sampling. We probe the effect of the two modes on the example of adenylate kinase, which exhibits a large conformational change upon substrate binding. Using BioEmu2 in structure prediction and equilibrium sampling mode, we generate conformations for the Apo (PDB structure 4AKE), the ATP-bound and the AMP+ATP-bound (PDB structure 1AKE) state (Fig. 3 a). In both modes, BioEmu2 samples structures close to the apo and the holo state, where the relative weight between sampled conformations shifts notably when adding ATP and AMP+ATP to the system, which is in line with experimentally measured PDB structures (stars). By switching between the modes, BioEmu2 transitions from narrowly distributed structure prediction to a continuously distributed ensemble of states, which captures the nature of thermal fluctuations in a biomolecular system. Using this setting, we compare BioEmu2 to a range of co-folding baseline models on the popular FoldBench benchmark suite [ 32 ] and the Runs N’ Poses benchmark [ 33 ] for protein–ligand bound structure prediction. We selected models for comparison that have a suitable commercial license (excludes AlphaFold3 [ 5 ] ) and a comparable training data cut-off (excludes Boltz-2 [ 39 ] ), resulting in the following baseline methods: Boltz-1 [ 28 ] , ESMFold2 [ 31 ] , OpenFold3 [ 40 ] , Protenix v1 and v2 [ 29 ] and OpenDDE [ 30 ] . We do not use confidence heads when aggregating over multiple samples. The full details of our versions of the two benchmarks are described in Sec. 4.8 . Across both benchmarks, BioEmu2 achieves accuracy competitive with the evaluated co-folding baselines, establishing structure prediction as a core capability of our model (Fig. 2 a,b). Specifically, in the FoldBench results we see that BioEmu2 achieves competitive lDDT [ 41 ] scores for protein and nucleic acid monomers, and attains strong DockQ-based [ 42 ] success rates for chain-to-chain binding. The higher score for protein–protein binding is likely driven by the training data composition, which emphasized protein–protein interaction. The protein–ligand evaluation from Runs N’ Poses also highlights the ability of BioEmu2 to model ligand placement alongside the surrounding protein structure [ 33 ] at a performance level comparable to other strong models. Illustrative predicted structures in colour, PDB ground truth in grey. a) Results on FoldBench, grouped by protein, RNA/DNA, protein complexes and protein–RNA/DNA complexes. Scaling inference to large complexes. BioEmu2’s structural prediction capability extends to larger molecular assemblies. To make larger biomolecular systems accessible at inference time, BioEmu2 implements context parallelism (CP) to distribute pair representations across multiple GPUs [ 43 ] . Benchmarks on NVIDIA B200 GPUs demonstrate scaling from a single GPU to 4 GPUs ( 2 × 2 2\times 2 ) and 16 GPUs ( 4 × 4 4\times 4 ) configurations, supporting systems of up to approximately 16,000 residues. Figure 2 c shows that our CP code substantially extends the maximum accessible system size with manageable communication overhead. At this size, the physicality of the prediction becomes more of a bottleneck than computational feasibility. BioEmu2 preserves both local structural accuracy and overall assembly organization for a wide range of large protein complexes containing thousands of residues. In this case, providing a few additional hints such as residue–residue contacts obtained from experimental knowledge can be sufficient to substantially improve BioEmu2’s predictions. As an example, for the 4,020-residue complex 8WY8, specifying just a single inter-chain contact dramatically improves prediction accuracy, reducing RMSD from 71.2 Å to 5.0 Å and increasing DockQ from 0.10 to 0.46 (Fig. 2 e). 3.2 Equilibrium Sampling In equilibrium mode, BioEmu2 generates independent draws from a learned structural distribution for the specified system. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.27911 (cs) [Submitted on 20 Nov 2026] Title: Functional Depth Is Learned: Isolating the Computation That Layers Produce Only Together Authors: JaeSeong Kim , KyungTae Lim View a PDF of the paper titled Functional Depth Is Learned: Isolating the Computation That Layers Produce Only Together, by JaeSeong Kim and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Transformer performance scales with depth, but layer count merely counts the opportunities for sequential computation: layers could still behave as nearly independent refinements that barely depend on one another. We study how transformers develop functional depth during pretraining, introducing an exact inclusion-exclusion decomposition that isolates the connected component, i.e., the computation that appears only when a specified set of layers acts together under identity ablation. Tracking this quantity across public checkpoints of Pythia, OLMo, and Amber yields three findings. First, write-relative connected coordination strengthens from its initialization or earliest-checkpoint baseline as pretraining proceeds, across all measured interaction orders. Second, these connected components are behaviorally consequential under direct intervention: deleting them damages perplexity more than deleting a norm-matched random direction at the same site in all 35 measured model-order cells. Third, pairwise representation similarity is consistently negatively correlated with pairwise connected coordination across seven models, yet the two signals are not interchangeable: similarity- and coordination-based block-removal criteria often agree in Pythia but diverge on Amber. Together, these results suggest that architectural depth provides the opportunity for sequential computation, while pretraining progressively organizes cross-layer dependencies within that depth. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.27899 (cs) [Submitted on 20 Nov 2026] Title: The Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework: Scalable Multimodal UX Attribution in Web Search Authors: Yi Ding , Gaurav Kumar , Rui Min , Isabella Ye , Bhavika Goyal , Emilio Antunez , Huihui Chen , Ke Xu , Xiaowei Sun , Xin Xu , Huijie Feng , Pradyumna Narayana , Golnaz Farhadi View a PDF of the paper titled The Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework: Scalable Multimodal UX Attribution in Web Search, by Yi Ding and 12 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Sustaining user experience (UX) quality in large-scale web search requires scalable evaluation. Traditional surveys are slow and bottleneck rapid A/B testing, while automated metrics often lack the granularity to diagnose visual-spatial UX anomalies. To address this, we introduce the Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework, a novel industrial architecture for automated UX attribution. Tier 1 (Macro System) acts as a scalable user sentiment regression detector, utilizing a fine-tuned encoder-decoder LLM (based on Gemini XS) on telemetry features. Through multi-task regularization and contextual feature engineering, this tier achieves a +9.8% PR-AUC gain on over 500,000 held-out records, matching baseline recall on all validated regressions with $\sim$20% relative precision gain among the 12 held-out experiments. In production, it reduces measurement latency from weeks to hours and cuts survey overhead by over 40%. Tier 2 (Micro System) provides granular diagnostics by employing a Multimodal LLM (Gemini 3.0 Pro) to natively assess visual renderings and spatial layout of web result blocks, quantifying "User Toil" as the estimated effort required to reach a satisfactory result. Enhanced by RL-based automated prompt optimization and an AI judge for win/loss patterns, the MLLM yields a $>$6.5% F1 score improvement, offering deep insights into content quality and layout friction. Ultimately, this framework enables scalable, accurate, and diagnostic UX attribution, processing O(100k) live experiment queries daily.
