items.content: The Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework: Scalable Multimodal UX Attribution in Web Search Yi Ding † † thanks: Corresponding author. Gaurav Kumar Rui Min Isabella Ye Bhavika Goyal Emilio Antunez Huihui Chen Ke Xu Xiaowei Sun Xin Xu Huijie Feng Pradyumna Narayana Golnaz Farhadi Abstract Sustaining user experience (UX) quality in large-scale web search requires scalable evaluation. Traditional surveys are slow and bottleneck rapid A/B testing, while automated metrics often lack the granularity to diagnose visual-spatial UX anomalies. To address this, we introduce the Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework, a novel industrial architecture for automated UX attribution. Tier 1 (Macro System) acts as a scalable user sentiment regression detector, utilizing a fine-tuned encoder-decoder LLM (based on Gemini XS) on telemetry features. Through multi-task regularization and contextual feature engineering, this tier achieves a +9.8% PR-AUC gain on over 500,000 held-out records, matching baseline recall on all validated regressions with around 20% relative precision gain among the 12 held-out experiments. In production, it reduces measurement latency from weeks to hours and cuts survey overhead by over 40%. Tier 2 (Micro System) provides granular diagnostics by employing a Multimodal LLM (Gemini 3.0 Pro) to natively assess visual renderings and spatial layout of web result blocks, quantifying “User Toil” as the estimated effort required to reach a satisfactory result. Enhanced by RL-based automated prompt optimization and an AI judge for win/loss patterns, the MLLM yields a >6.5% F1 score improvement, offering deep insights into content quality and layout friction. Ultimately, this framework enables scalable, accurate, and diagnostic UX attribution, processing O(100k) live experiment queries daily. Google, Mountain View, CA, USA ellading@google.com Introduction The continuous evolution of modern web search and advertising platforms is driven by massive, high-frequency A/B experiments ( Kohavi et al. 2020 ) . While these rapid release cycles are essential for product innovation, accurately capturing how users subjectively experience these changes at scale remains a critical industry challenge. Exposing users to localized layout friction or visual degradation erodes platform trust and diminishes long-term engagement. Consequently, developing sophisticated, automated systems to evaluate User Experience (UX) is essential. A central difficulty in this domain is the challenge of scalable Multi-modal UX Attribution. In a production environment, evaluating search satisfaction presents distinct hurdles compared to traditional offline, text-based relevance scoring: • The Latency and Scalability Bottleneck: Human-in-the-loop surveys provide qualitative insights but are fundamentally unscalable. Relying on human annotators delays the assessment of live experiments by weeks and is susceptible to inherent rater noise and response bias ( Karpinska et al. 2021 ) . • The Diagnostic Gap in Aggregated Telemetry: Automated telemetry (e.g., clicks) provides necessary global safeguards but lacks the granularity to explain why a regression occurred. Standard logs struggle to detect visual-spatial UX anomalies that result in user friction in the subjective browsing journey. Legacy heuristic DOM-based baselines (e.g., element density or scroll depth) are similarly insufficient because they fail to capture semantic visual friction, such as distinguishing an ad that is structurally identical in the DOM yet visually distinct (e.g., featuring a subtle ‘Sponsored’ badge) from an organic result. • Multimodal Complexity: Modern Search Result Pages (SRPs) are complex visual structures. Assessing user sentiment requires bridging sparse behavioral logs with the multimodal nature of the rendered page structure. Figure 1: The Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework. Experiments are evaluated in parallel: Tier 1 safeguards against whole-page sentiment regressions, while Tier 2 validates fine-granular improvements in User Toil. A strict launch gate requires both conditions to be met. To overcome these limitations and bridge the gap between scale and granularity, we introduce the Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework , an industrial evaluation architecture for offline measurement (Figure 1 ). Rather than a simple sequential triage, this framework defines a strict, dual-criteria launch paradigm by running two synergistic systems in parallel: Tier 1 (Macro System) functions as a global safeguard, providing regression assessment of the user’s general sentiment across the whole page. We designed a dual-head LLM based on Gemini XS (a model with 𝒪 \mathcal{O} (billions) of parameters) fine-tuned from historical user survey responses. The encoder predicts a user satisfaction score based on a rich suite of lexical, structural, and behavioral telemetry features, while the decoder generates Chain-of-Thought (CoT) ( Wei et al. 2022 ) rationales distilled from a larger teacher model. This model ingests lexical context, quantitative metadata, and aggregate user interaction signals to accurately flag broad sentiment regressions. Tier 2 (Micro System) operates as a fine-granular assessment platform. It utilizes a prompt-based Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM), specifically Gemini 3.0 Pro, to assess visual renderings of result blocks alongside personalized query contexts. By parsing spatial behavior and visual clarity directly from rendered pages, it actively measures improvements in localized “User Toil.” To ensure rigorous evaluation and establish a reliable ground truth, we leverage an AI-as-a-Judge approach for side-by-side (SxS) comparisons, which bootstraps a high-quality human-annotated dataset and actively refines our human rating guidelines. We further enhance Tier 2’s robustness in production through a novel Mentor-Student framework optimized with reinforcement learning (RL) for automated prompt generation. Ultimately, an A/B experiment is only approved for production launch from a user sentiment perspective if it achieves fine-granular UX improvement via the Micro System without whole-page regressions in the Macro System. This dual-requirement is necessary because the two tiers do not always align; the Macro System is less sensitive to granular quality changes, resulting in experiments that yield neutral Tier 1 results despite meaningful metric movements in Tier 2. In summary, our main contributions are: • A Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework that redefines launch criteria at scale ( 𝒪 ⁡ ( 100 ​ k ) \mathcal{O}(100\text{k}) queries/day) by requiring both whole-page sentiment stability and granular visual UX improvements. • Deployment of a dual-head, CoT-distilled LLM (Gemini XS Macro System) that reduces measurement latency from weeks to hours and cuts survey overhead by over 40%. • An MLLM evaluation pipeline leveraging an AI-as-a-Judge for side-by-side (SxS) comparisons, which facilitates the construction of a high-quality human-annotated dataset. • An RL-optimized Mentor-Student prompting strategy for MLLMs (Gemini 3.0 Pro) along with the AI-as-a-Judge. Related Work Traditional search result quality evaluation has historically relied on implicit behavioral click models and utility metrics, which often miss the complex visual layouts and cognitive friction of modern web navigation ( Borisov et al. 2018 ; Shi et al. 2025 ) . Consequently, recent academic efforts have transitioned to Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Architectures such as UGround ( Gou et al. 2025 ) and Aria-UI ( Yang et al. 2025 ) show that grounding raw bounding box coordinates significantly enhances pixel-level spatial understanding ( Chen et al. 2023 ) . However, these models typically evaluate isolated screenshots in controlled environments and lack mechanisms to capture dynamic pre-click scanning effort or post-click user toil. Moreover, recent benchmarking of MLLMs as UI evaluators ( Luera et al. 2025 ) reveals that off-the-shelf models align with human judgments on some UI dimensions but break down on others. This validates our Tier 2 design: because base MLLMs struggle with specific UI nuances out-of-the-box, zero-shot inference is insufficient. We overcome this by utilizing RL Mentor-Student tuning and AI Judge alignment to capture complex visual-spatial dimensions where standard MLLMs typically fail. Industrial high-throughput classifiers often sacrifice interpretability for latency. Recent architectures address this by leveraging large teacher models to distill Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning into lightweight student models ( Kumar et al. 2026 ) . Advanced multi-task learning paradigms, such as Dual-Head Reasoning Distillation (DHRD), further utilize this CoT rationale generation solely as a train-time regularizer, boosting accuracy without inference delays ( Xu et al. 2025 ) . Additionally, while automated evaluation frameworks like CLEAR efficiently cluster systemic LLM-as-a-judge errors ( Yehudai et al. 2026 ) , and discrete Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods like RLPrompt optimize black-box model instructions ( Deng et al. 2022 ) , these tools are typically benchmarked on deterministic reasoning tasks. They lack the cohesive integration needed to resolve the ambiguity and subjectivity of human UX sentiment. Our proposed framework bridges this gap. System Design and Implementation To quantify user satisfaction as described in the dual-criteria launch paradigm introduced in Section 1, our architecture evaluates live experiment traffic through two synergistic pipelines. The Macro System (Tier 1) operates on aggregate telemetry to provide a high-throughput global safeguard against sentiment degradation. Concurrently, the Micro System (Tier 2) leverages multimodal capabilities to diagnose spatial and temporal friction when navigating through web search results. Tier 1: Macro Sentiment Detection The Macro System serves as the first line of defense, computing aggregate user satisfaction scores across control and treatment arms to detect whole-page experience degradation with statistical significance. Dual-Head Model Architecture Operating as the framework’s primary screening mechanism, Tier 1 must support an inference throughput of 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 ​ M ) \mathcal{O}(1\text{M}) queries. By rapidly identifying experiments that cause whole-page sentiment degradation, this tier acts as an early-stopping gate—effectively bypassing the need for slow, costly human surveys and avoiding computationally intensive visual analysis in Tier 2. To achieve this scale under strict production latency constraints, we designed a hybrid encoder-decoder architecture that processes only lightweight, text-based modalities. To balance predictive accuracy with interpretability, we separate the tasks across two distinct heads: the encoder functions as a discriminatory classifier predicting binary user sentiment (Regression vs. No Regression), while the decoder is tasked with generating Chain-of-Thought (CoT) rationales. During the training phase, the reasoning targets are distilled from a massive “teacher” model that processes historical human survey responses and rich text features. During live inference, the encoder head directly outputs sentiment predictions while the decoder concurrently synthesizes reasoning. Crucially, the multi-task learning signal from the decoder’s CoT generation acts as a structural regularizer. This dual-head paradigm improves the encoder’s predictive Precision-Recall Area Under Curve (PR-AUC) by an absolute margin of +2.0%. Feature Representations To capture the nuanced context of search and advertising, the macro model ingests three distinct categories of sparse telemetry: • Lexical Context (TEXT) (Base textual representations, encompassing the search query text, sponsored ad titles, and organic search snippets). • Quantitative Metadata (QF) (Query-level structural features, including ad density, commercial load, match types, and high-level UI layout configurations). • Aggregate User Interactions Features (UF) (Aggregate behavioral signals reflecting engagement, such as click-through rates, and post-click abandonment). Tier 2: Micro Diagnostic System Figure 2: Four-stage diagnostic execution pipeline for computing whole-page User Toil. While Tier 1 captures telemetry-driven regressions, it lacks the spatial awareness to diagnose why a visual UI change frustrated a user and how to attribute the root cause on a fine-granular level. The Micro System complements this limitation by quantifying the granular, multimodal friction—termed User Toil —that individuals experience when navigating a Search Results Page (SRP). This is achieved through a structured, four-stage execution pipeline (Figure 2 ). 1. Sample SRP & Annotate: The pipeline samples visual renderings from live traffic and annotates exact pixel bounding-box coordinates for each distinct result block. 2. Context Enrichment: Raw visual renderings are enriched with (a) Visual Context via the rendered representation of result blocks; (b) Refined Query Intent (RQI) distilled from aggregate past history; and (c) Result-Specific Context , a semantic summary of its associated Landing Page (LP). 3. Autorate Satisfaction: An MLLM ingests the enriched contexts to evaluate intent alignment, semantic relevance, and visual clarity, assigning each block an ordinal satisfaction rating. 4. Compute Whole-Page User Toil: Finally, the pipeline aggregates these discrete ratings into the holistic User Toil metric, simulating the chronological friction of the user’s browsing journey. Parameterizing the User Toil Metric The core philosophy of User Toil is to estimate the total cognitive and temporal effort required for a user to scan a page and interact with results until they reach their first “Very Satisfied” (VS) outcome. We define User Toil ( T T ) as: T = ∑ i ∈ Results { ( t scan ( x i , y i ) + t friction ( L P i ) ) ⋅ 𝕀 ( i ≤ idx VS ) } \begin{split}T&=\sum_{i\in\text{Results}}\bigg\{\Big(t_{\text{scan}}(x_{i},y_{i})\\ &\quad+t_{\text{friction}}(LP_{i})\Big)\cdot\mathbb{I}(i\leq\text{idx}_{\text{VS}})\bigg\}\end{split} (1) where 𝕀 \mathbb{I} is an indicator function that truncates the summation once the user encounters the first Highly Satisfactory result ( idx VS \text{idx}_{\text{VS}} ), assuming their core search intent has been fulfilled. The two primary components are parameterized as follows: • t scan ​ ( x i , y i ) t_{\text{scan}}(x_{i},y_{i}) models pre-click visual scanning effort . It is parameterized by the bounding box coordinates ( x i , y i ) (x_{i},y_{i}) of result i i . Blocks positioned lower on the page (high y y -coordinate) or buried in dense visual clusters incur a higher t scan t_{\text{scan}} penalty due to the required visual parsing. • t friction ​ ( L ​ P i ) t_{\text{friction}}(LP_{i}) models post-click cognitive load . It represents the estimated time wasted exploring a result. If a clicked landing page ( L ​ P i LP_{i} ) is irrelevant, clickbait, or difficult to navigate, the MLLM assigns a high t friction t_{\text{friction}} penalty. Conversely, an immediately relevant page incurs minimal friction. To illustrate the practical application of the User Toil metric ( T T ), consider a user searching for “noise-canceling headphones”. 1. Result 1 (Top Sponsored Product): Appears at the top of the viewport. The estimated pre-click visual scan cost t scan t_{\text{scan}} is near zero. Upon interaction, the landing page is out-of-stock and difficult to navigate. The MLLM, analyzing the rendered landing page content, rates this outcome as "Dissatisfied," assigning a high post-click friction cost, t friction = 15 t_{\text{friction}}=15 units. 2. Result 2 (Organic List): Positioned lower on the page, requiring an estimated pre-click visual scan cost of t scan = 3 t_{\text{scan}}=3 units based on its vertical position and surrounding layout density. The landing page content has the exact desired product. The MLLM rates this as "Very Satisfied," with t friction = 0 t_{\text{friction}}=0 . The total estimated User Toil for this page is ( 0 + 15 ) + ( 3 + 0 ) = 18 (0+15)+(3+0)=18 . If a UI experiment moved Result 2 to the top, a user would likely interact with it first. The new estimated Toil would drop to ( 0 + 0 ) = 0 (0+0)=0 , quantitatively demonstrating a significant UX improvement. The costs per result are model-based estimates derived from the visual rendering and content, not direct measurements of individual user behavior. We do not use raw per-session dwell times as ground-truth, since they introduce severe heavy-tailed variance. For example, idle browser tabs or extended reading on informational pages conflate benign engagement with UX friction and inflate experiment confidence intervals. Specifically, these units act as ordinal penalty scores weighted by historical timing distributions. Through an offline calibration mapping, the discrete categorical outputs of the MLLM (e.g., “Dissatisfied”) are mapped to numerical penalty weights that reflect the relative magnitude of time-wasting observed in historical log distributions. Consequently, a reduction in User Toil serves as an ordinal threshold for our launch gate rather than a literal budget of measured seconds. In offline stability checks, directional experiment-level Toil movements and Tier 2 launch recommendations remain stable across alternative aggregations of historical penalty weights that preserve ordinal monotonicity. Iterative Alignment and Prompt Optimization To ensure the Micro System accurately reflects complex human subjectivity, we designed an automated alignment architecture that continuously refines the MLLM’s behavior without requiring full-parameter fine-tuning. AI-as-a-Judge for Loss Pattern Analysis We implemented an auxiliary MLLM (Gemini 3.0 Pro) equipped with toolkits for Google Search and URL context parsing to act as an “AI Judge” for Side-by-Side (SxS) evaluation. By ingesting human rating guidelines alongside the outputs of both human experts and our autorater, the AI Judge systematically clusters failure patterns. For instance, the Judge identified that early iterations of our baseline struggled to distinguish boundaries in complex carousels (e.g. UI elements that group multiple individual result cards horizontally). This specific diagnostic insight drove the architectural decision to inject exact pixel bounding boxes into the prompt, yielding an immediate +5% F1 improvement against human ground truth. RL-Based Prompt Optimization Figure 3: Dual-agent RL-based Automated Prompt Optimization flow. To scale this alignment, we deployed a dual-agent Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework ( Sayana et al. 2026 ) to automate prompt construction (Figure 3 ). Dual-Agent Dynamics: The architecture consists of a Mentor (a lightweight, highly efficient model) and a Student (a massive, frozen reasoning engine). The Mentor does not evaluate sentiment; instead, it functions as a strategic controller, learning a policy ( π θ \pi_{\theta} ) to formulate optimal, task-specific system instructions ( p p ) token-by-token. The Student acts as the worker agent, executing these instructions to rate the SRP. Standardizing execution on a frozen Student ensures the backbone retains its broad multimodal capabilities without risking catastrophic forgetting. Optimization Regime: We formulate the optimization of the Mentor policy π θ \pi_{\theta} as an RL problem over a discrete token action space: max θ 𝔼 x ∼ 𝒟 , p ∼ π θ ( ⋅ | x ) [ R ( x , p , y ) − β 𝔻 K ​ L ( π θ ∥ π ref ) ] \max_{\theta}\,\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},p\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}\Big[R(x,p,y)-\beta\mathbb{D}_{KL}\left(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\text{ref}}\right)\Big] (2) where x x is the input context, y y is the ground truth human rating, p p is the generated prompt, 𝔻 K ​ L \mathbb{D}_{KL} is the Kullback-Leibler divergence to prevent policy collapse, and β \beta is the regularization coefficient. A unique challenge in UX evaluation is optimizing a single query-level prompt ( p p ) that must accurately evaluate multiple, distinct results on the same page. To preserve this structural hierarchy, we design the reward R R as the arithmetic mean of the individual result rewards r i r_{i} (where r i r_{i} reflects the MLLM’s accuracy against the human rating for result i i ): R = 1 n ​ ∑ i = 1 n r i R=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{i} . It ensures that the Mentor is uniformly incentivized to generate instructions that improve the Student’s diagnostic accuracy across the entire web page, effectively bridging the gap between automated telemetry and subjective human experience. The RL training is performed entirely offline to remove prompt-generation variance in production: once π θ \pi_{\theta} converges, the single highest-scoring discrete system prompt p ∗ p^{*} (selected on a held-out validation split) is frozen and deployed to the Student MLLM. The student MLLM also utilizes deterministic greedy decoding configurations ( e.g. temperature = 0 \text{e.g. temperature}=0 ) to remove sampling variance in its outputs during production A/B evaluation. Experimental Methodology and Results To validate the Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework, we designed an evaluation methodology that mirrors its production deployment: Tier 1 is evaluated on its ability to act as a high-throughput, high-recall regression net, while Tier 2 is evaluated on its diagnostic precision against human-perceived visual friction. Tier 1: Macro User Sentiment Detection Dataset: Survey-Backed Telemetry Evaluating subjective user friction at a whole-page scope requires proprietary datasets that accurately reflect real-world UI complexity. Ground truth labels for Tier 1 were derived from in-product user surveys triggered after a few minutes of active search session time. To ensure robust generalization, the Macro model was trained on data from 11 distinct A/B experiments. It was rigorously evaluated on a holdout suite of 12 unseen experiments collected strictly after the model checkpoint was frozen. This evaluation dataset comprises > 500,000 >500,000 records sampled evenly across control and treatment arms to calculate experiment-level precision and recall. Ablation and Impact Model Architecture / Features Δ \Delta PR-AUC Baseline Lexical features (TEXT) (Ref) + Decoder TEXT + Teacher CoT +2.0% + Metadata TEXT + Query Features (QF) +5.1% + User Sigs TEXT + QF + User Features (UF) +9.8% Table 1: Ablation Study on Macro System Architecture. We fine-tuned the Macro Model using PR-AUC as our primary metric to account for class imbalances in sentiment degradation. Extensive ablation studies (Table 1 ) quantify our architectural decisions. The baseline model, utilizing solely lexical features (TEXT), served as the reference and represents the prior production incumbent deployed on the same training data. Introducing the dual-head CoT regularizer brought an immediate +2.0% PR-AUC gain. The sequential integration of Quantitative Metadata (QF) and Aggregated User Interactions Features (UF) signals pushed the peak performance gain to +9.8% over the baseline. Translating Metrics to Operational Impact: This +9.8% PR-AUC gain fundamentally alters the A/B testing lifecycle: We define a sentiment regression as a statistically significant degradation in the aggregated user satisfaction metric (treatment versus control), verified using a required volume of events. Under this definition, Tier 1 successfully yields no missed regressions among the 4 validated positive regressions across the 12 held-out experiments. Furthermore, precision is evaluated at the experiment level: at the operational gating threshold, the baseline model flagged 6 experiments (yielding a precision of 66.7%, i.e., 4/6), while the final dual-head Macro System flagged 5 experiments, yielding a precision of 80% (4/5)—an effective ∼ \sim 20% relative detection precision improvement. Related Work Traditional search result quality evaluation has historically relied on implicit behavioral click models and utility metrics, which often miss the complex visual layouts and cognitive friction of modern web navigation ( Borisov et al. 2018 ; Shi et al. 2025 ) . Consequently, recent academic efforts have transitioned to Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Architectures such as UGround ( Gou et al. 2025 ) and Aria-UI ( Yang et al. 2025 ) show that grounding raw bounding box coordinates significantly enhances pixel-level spatial understanding ( Chen et al. 2023 ) . However, these models typically evaluate isolated screenshots in controlled environments and lack mechanisms to capture dynamic pre-click scanning effort or post-click user toil. Moreover, recent benchmarking of MLLMs as UI evaluators ( Luera et al. 2025 ) reveals that off-the-shelf models align with human judgments on some UI dimensions but break down on others. This validates our Tier 2 design: because base MLLMs struggle with specific UI nuances out-of-the-box, zero-shot inference is insufficient. We overcome this by utilizing RL Mentor-Student tuning and AI Judge alignment to capture complex visual-spatial dimensions where standard MLLMs typically fail. Industrial high-throughput classifiers often sacrifice interpretability for latency. Recent architectures address this by leveraging large teacher models to distill Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning into lightweight student models ( Kumar et al. 2026 ) . Advanced multi-task learning paradigms, such as Dual-Head Reasoning Distillation (DHRD), further utilize this CoT rationale generation solely as a train-time regularizer, boosting accuracy without inference delays ( Xu et al. 2025 ) . Additionally, while automated evaluation frameworks like CLEAR efficiently cluster systemic LLM-as-a-judge errors ( Yehudai et al. 2026 ) , and discrete Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods like RLPrompt optimize black-box model instructions ( Deng et al. 2022 ) , these tools are typically benchmarked on deterministic reasoning tasks. They lack the cohesive integration needed to resolve the ambiguity and subjectivity of human UX sentiment. Our proposed framework bridges this gap. System Design and Implementation To quantify user satisfaction as described in the dual-criteria launch paradigm introduced in Section 1, our architecture evaluates live experiment traffic through two synergistic pipelines. The Macro System (Tier 1) operates on aggregate telemetry to provide a high-throughput global safeguard against sentiment degradation. Concurrently, the Micro System (Tier 2) leverages multimodal capabilities to diagnose spatial and temporal friction when navigating through web search results. Tier 1: Macro Sentiment Detection The Macro System serves as the first line of defense, computing aggregate user satisfaction scores across control and treatment arms to detect whole-page experience degradation with statistical significance. Dual-Head Model Architecture Operating as the framework’s primary screening mechanism, Tier 1 must support an inference throughput of 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 ​ M ) \mathcal{O}(1\text{M}) queries. By rapidly identifying experiments that cause whole-page sentiment degradation, this tier acts as an early-stopping gate—effectively bypassing the need for slow, costly human surveys and avoiding computationally intensive visual analysis in Tier 2. To achieve this scale under strict production latency constraints, we designed a hybrid encoder-decoder architecture that processes only lightweight, text-based modalities. To balance predictive accuracy with interpretability, we separate the tasks across two distinct heads: the encoder functions as a discriminatory classifier predicting binary user sentiment (Regression vs. No Regression), while the decoder is tasked with generating Chain-of-Thought (CoT) rationales. During the training phase, the reasoning targets are distilled from a massive “teacher” model that processes historical human survey responses and rich text features. During live inference, the encoder head directly outputs sentiment predictions while the decoder concurrently synthesizes reasoning. Crucially, the multi-task learning signal from the decoder’s CoT generation acts as a structural regularizer. This dual-head paradigm improves the encoder’s predictive Precision-Recall Area Under Curve (PR-AUC) by an absolute margin of +2.0%. Feature Representations To capture the nuanced context of search and advertising, the macro model ingests three distinct categories of sparse telemetry: • Lexical Context (TEXT) (Base textual representations, encompassing the search query text, sponsored ad titles, and organic search snippets). • Quantitative Metadata (QF) (Query-level structural features, including ad density, commercial load, match types, and high-level UI layout configurations). • Aggregate User Interactions Features (UF) (Aggregate behavioral signals reflecting engagement, such as click-through rates, and post-click abandonment). Tier 2: Micro Diagnostic System Figure 2: Four-stage diagnostic execution pipeline for computing whole-page User Toil. While Tier 1 captures telemetry-driven regressions, it lacks the spatial awareness to diagnose why a visual UI change frustrated a user and how to attribute the root cause on a fine-granular level. The Micro System complements this limitation by quantifying the granular, multimodal friction—termed User Toil —that individuals experience when navigating a Search Results Page (SRP). This is achieved through a structured, four-stage execution pipeline (Figure 2 ). 1. Sample SRP & Annotate: The pipeline samples visual renderings from live traffic and annotates exact pixel bounding-box coordinates for each distinct result block. 2. Context Enrichment: Raw visual renderings are enriched with (a) Visual Context via the rendered representation of result blocks; (b) Refined Query Intent (RQI) distilled from aggregate past history; and (c) Result-Specific Context , a semantic summary of its associated Landing Page (LP). 3. Autorate Satisfaction: An MLLM ingests the enriched contexts to evaluate intent alignment, semantic relevance, and visual clarity, assigning each block an ordinal satisfaction rating. 4. Compute Whole-Page User Toil: Finally, the pipeline aggregates these discrete ratings into the holistic User Toil metric, simulating the chronological friction of the user’s browsing journey. Parameterizing the User Toil Metric The core philosophy of User Toil is to estimate the total cognitive and temporal effort required for a user to scan a page and interact with results until they reach their first “Very Satisfied” (VS) outcome. We define User Toil ( T T ) as: T = ∑ i ∈ Results { ( t scan ( x i , y i ) + t friction ( L P i ) ) ⋅ 𝕀 ( i ≤ idx VS ) } \begin{split}T&=\sum_{i\in\text{Results}}\bigg\{\Big(t_{\text{scan}}(x_{i},y_{i})\\ &\quad+t_{\text{friction}}(LP_{i})\Big)\cdot\mathbb{I}(i\leq\text{idx}_{\text{VS}})\bigg\}\end{split} (1) where 𝕀 \mathbb{I} is an indicator function that truncates the summation once the user encounters the first Highly Satisfactory result ( idx VS \text{idx}_{\text{VS}} ), assuming their core search intent has been fulfilled. The two primary components are parameterized as follows: • t scan ​ ( x i , y i ) t_{\text{scan}}(x_{i},y_{i}) models pre-click visual scanning effort . It is parameterized by the bounding box coordinates ( x i , y i ) (x_{i},y_{i}) of result i i . Blocks positioned lower on the page (high y y -coordinate) or buried in dense visual clusters incur a higher t scan t_{\text{scan}} penalty due to the required visual parsing. • t friction ​ ( L ​ P i ) t_{\text{friction}}(LP_{i}) models post-click cognitive load . It represents the estimated time wasted exploring a result. If a clicked landing page ( L ​ P i LP_{i} ) is irrelevant, clickbait, or difficult to navigate, the MLLM assigns a high t friction t_{\text{friction}} penalty. Conversely, an immediately relevant page incurs minimal friction. To illustrate the practical application of the User Toil metric ( T T ), consider a user searching for “noise-canceling headphones”. 1. Result 1 (Top Sponsored Product): Appears at the top of the viewport. The estimated pre-click visual scan cost t scan t_{\text{scan}} is near zero. Upon interaction, the landing page is out-of-stock and difficult to navigate. The MLLM, analyzing the rendered landing page content, rates this outcome as "Dissatisfied," assigning a high post-click friction cost, t friction = 15 t_{\text{friction}}=15 units. 2. Result 2 (Organic List): Positioned lower on the page, requiring an estimated pre-click visual scan cost of t scan = 3 t_{\text{scan}}=3 units based on its vertical position and surrounding layout density. The landing page content has the exact desired product. The MLLM rates this as "Very Satisfied," with t friction = 0 t_{\text{friction}}=0 . The total estimated User Toil for this page is ( 0 + 15 ) + ( 3 + 0 ) = 18 (0+15)+(3+0)=18 . If a UI experiment moved Result 2 to the top, a user would likely interact with it first. The new estimated Toil would drop to ( 0 + 0 ) = 0 (0+0)=0 , quantitatively demonstrating a significant UX improvement. The costs per result are model-based estimates derived from the visual rendering and content, not direct measurements of individual user behavior. We do not use raw per-session dwell times as ground-truth, since they introduce severe heavy-tailed variance. For example, idle browser tabs or extended reading on informational pages conflate benign engagement with UX friction and inflate experiment confidence intervals. Specifically, these units act as ordinal penalty scores weighted by historical timing distributions. Through an offline calibration mapping, the discrete categorical outputs of the MLLM (e.g., “Dissatisfied”) are mapped to numerical penalty weights that reflect the relative magnitude of time-wasting observed in historical log distributions. Consequently, a reduction in User Toil serves as an ordinal threshold for our launch gate rather than a literal budget of measured seconds. In offline stability checks, directional experiment-level Toil movements and Tier 2 launch recommendations remain stable across alternative aggregations of historical penalty weights that preserve ordinal monotonicity. Iterative Alignment and Prompt Optimization To ensure the Micro System accurately reflects complex human subjectivity, we designed an automated alignment architecture that continuously refines the MLLM’s behavior without requiring full-parameter fine-tuning. AI-as-a-Judge for Loss Pattern Analysis We implemented an auxiliary MLLM (Gemini 3.0 Pro) equipped with toolkits for Google Search and URL context parsing to act as an “AI Judge” for Side-by-Side (SxS) evaluation. By ingesting human rating guidelines alongside the outputs of both human experts and our autorater, the AI Judge systematically clusters failure patterns. For instance, the Judge identified that early iterations of our baseline struggled to distinguish boundaries in complex carousels (e.g. UI elements that group multiple individual result cards horizontally). This specific diagnostic insight drove the architectural decision to inject exact pixel bounding boxes into the prompt, yielding an immediate +5% F1 improvement against human ground truth. RL-Based Prompt Optimization Figure 3: Dual-agent RL-based Automated Prompt Optimization flow. To scale this alignment, we deployed a dual-agent Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework ( Sayana et al. 2026 ) to automate prompt construction (Figure 3 ). Dual-Agent Dynamics: The architecture consists of a Mentor (a lightweight, highly efficient model) and a Student (a massive, frozen reasoning engine). The Mentor does not evaluate sentiment; instead, it functions as a strategic controller, learning a policy ( π θ \pi_{\theta} ) to formulate optimal, task-specific system instructions ( p p ) token-by-token. The Student acts as the worker agent, executing these instructions to rate the SRP. Standardizing execution on a frozen Student ensures the backbone retains its broad multimodal capabilities without risking catastrophic forgetting. Optimization Regime: We formulate the optimization of the Mentor policy π θ \pi_{\theta} as an RL problem over a discrete token action space: max θ 𝔼 x ∼ 𝒟 , p ∼ π θ ( ⋅ | x ) [ R ( x , p , y ) − β 𝔻 K ​ L ( π θ ∥ π ref ) ] \max_{\theta}\,\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},p\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}\Big[R(x,p,y)-\beta\mathbb{D}_{KL}\left(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\text{ref}}\right)\Big] (2) where x x is the input context, y y is the ground truth human rating, p p is the generated prompt, 𝔻 K ​ L \mathbb{D}_{KL} is the Kullback-Leibler divergence to prevent policy collapse, and β \beta is the regularization coefficient. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.27891 (cs) [Submitted on 20 Nov 2026] Title: Speculative Decoding Is Less Speculative Than You Think Authors: Guanning Zeng , Andrea Zanette View a PDF of the paper titled Speculative Decoding Is Less Speculative Than You Think, by Guanning Zeng and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model inference by preparing candidate continuations before the target model generates them. Its efficiency depends on how well limited drafting computation anticipates the path the target will actually follow. Anticipating this path involves two sources of uncertainty: the target model's predictions and the randomness of sampling. Yet the former requires a target-model forward pass, while the latter can be fixed before drafting. Building on this observation, we introduce DICE (Draw-Informed Candidate Selection), which pre-samples and synchronizes verification randomness across drafting and verification. By combining these known draws with predictions from an existing drafter, DICE allocates computation toward continuations more likely to be used in the current sampling run. This principle guides node selection throughout draft-tree construction and extends to asynchronous prefetching, where DICE predicts which next-round drafts to prepare. Without additional drafter training or changes to the target sampling distribution, DICE achieves state-of-the-art decoding throughput across diverse settings, with speedups of up to 24.6pp over strong baselines.
